The exercise is about scale. Zooming out shrinks our worries and our self-importance together. It's not meant to make you feel worthless, but to put your concerns in proportion.

Today: when something feels huge, picture it against the size of the world and the length of history.
meditations-5.25:
Someone wrongs me? That's their concern, Marcus says. They have their own character and their own actions. I have what nature wants me to have right now, and I do what my nature wants me to do.

It's a clean division of responsibility. Their wrongdoing is theirs to answer for. Your job is your own response, which stays fully yours.

Today: when someone behaves badly, say to yourself, 'that's theirs; my part is how I respond.'
meditations-5.26:
Let the ruling part of your mind stay undisturbed by bodily pleasure and pain, Marcus says. Don't let it merge with them; keep them confined to where they belong. When sensations do reach the mind, as they naturally will since body and mind are one system, don't try to deny them. But don't let the mind add the opinion that they're good or bad.

This is a careful position. Stoics don't pretend not to feel pain. They separate the sensation, which is natural, from the judgment 'this is terrible', which is optional.

Today: when you feel discomfort, notice the sensation without adding a verdict to it.
meditations-5.27:
Live with the gods, Marcus says. And you do that by showing them that your soul is content with what it's given, and does what the daemon wants: the guardian and guide Zeus gave each person, a fragment of himself. That daemon is each person's mind and reason.

For Stoics, the divine isn't far away; your own reason is a piece of it. Living well and living with the gods turn out to be the same thing: using that reason well and accepting your lot.

Today: act on one decision you've reasoned through, rather than one you've drifted into.
meditations-5.28:
Are you angry at someone because their armpits stink or their breath smells? Marcus asks. What good does that do? That's how their body is. 'But they have reason; they could figure out what's offensive.' Good for you. You have reason too: use yours to awaken theirs. Point out the problem, kindly. If they listen, you've cured it, and anger was never needed.

He's using a deliberately petty example for a bigger point: anger at people's flaws is useless, and gentle correction works better.

The bracketed aside at the end, 'neither tragic actor nor whore', is a fragment whose meaning is unclear.

Today: instead of being irritated by someone's habit, mention it to them kindly or let it go.
enchiridion-14:
If you want your children, spouse and friends to live forever, Epictetus says, you're foolish: you want what's not in your power to be in your power. Wanting your servant to have no faults is equally foolish: you want vice to be something other than vice. But if you want not to be disappointed, that is in your power.

A person's master is whoever can give or take away what that person wants or fears. So whoever wants to be free should want nothing and avoid nothing that depends on others. Otherwise they'll be a slave.

Today: notice who has power over you through what you want, and loosen that want.
meditations-5.29:
However you plan to live when you've left all this, Marcus says, you can live that way here. And if people won't let you, then leave life, but without feeling wronged. 'The house is smoky, so I leave it.' Why make a fuss?

But as long as nothing drives him out, he stays, free, and no one can stop him choosing to act as a rational, social being.

The Stoics allowed that life could become unbearable. But the emphasis here is on staying and living freely; the smoky-house image is meant to drain the drama from the idea.

Today: live one hour the way you imagine your ideal self would.
meditations-5.30:
The mind of the universe is social, Marcus says. It made lesser things for the sake of greater ones, and fitted the greater ones to one another. Look how it has arranged and coordinated everything, given each its share, and brought the best things into harmony.

For the Stoics, cooperation isn't just a human virtue but the structure of reality. Rational beings are made to fit together, like parts of a well-designed whole.

Today: find one way to fit your efforts together with someone else's.
meditations-5.31:
Marcus runs an inventory. How have you treated the gods, your parents, siblings, children, teachers, those who cared for you as a baby, friends, relatives, servants? Have you behaved so that it could be said of you, as Homer said of someone, that you never wronged anyone in deed or word?

Then he looks back: how much you've been through and endured, that your story is nearly complete and your service done, how many beautiful things you've seen, how many pleasures and pains you've looked past, how many honors you've declined, and how many ill-natured people you've been kind to.

Today: pick one person from his list and ask how well you've treated them.
meditations-5.32:
Why should unskilled, ignorant souls disturb someone who has skill and knowledge? Marcus asks. And which soul has skill and knowledge? The one that understands beginnings and ends, and the reason that runs through all things and governs the universe through time.

The suggestion is that being disturbed by foolish people is a sign you've forgotten the bigger picture. Understanding how things work should make their behavior less upsetting, not more.

Today: when someone's ignorance irritates you, remember that understanding is meant to make you calmer, not angrier.
meditations-5.33:
Soon you'll be ashes or bones, Marcus says, a name or not even that, and a name is just sound and echo. What people value is hollow and petty: like puppies biting each other, or children squabbling, laughing and then crying. Faithfulness, modesty, justice and truth have fled the earth, as the poet said.

So why stay? The senses deceive, the soul is fragile, and reputation in such a world is empty. Wait calmly for the end, whatever it is. Until then, what's enough? Honor the gods, do good to people, practice patience and self-restraint, and remember that everything beyond your own body and breath isn't yours to control.

Today: do one good thing for someone, and let the rest go.
meditations-5.34:
You can live in a steady flow of happiness, Marcus says, if you take the right path and think and act rightly. Two things are shared by God, humans and every rational being: not being blocked by anyone else, and finding the good in a just disposition and just action, and letting your desire end there.

The happiness he describes is self-contained. It doesn't depend on circumstances, because it rests on how you choose to act, which no one else can stop.

Today: measure your day by whether you acted justly, not by how it went.
meditations-5.35:
If this isn't my own wrongdoing, or the result of it, Marcus asks, and the community isn't harmed, why am I upset? And what harm is there to the community?

It's a two-question test. Is it my fault? Does it hurt anyone? If the answer to both is no, the distress has no real basis. It's a quick way to sort genuine problems from mere irritations.

Today: run one frustration through both questions.
meditations-5.36:
Don't be swept along by how things look, Marcus says. Help people as you can and as they deserve, but if they've lost things that don't really matter, don't treat it as real damage; that's a bad habit. Be like the old man in a story who, when leaving, asked for his foster child's toy top back, knowing it was just a top.

Then he pictures himself shouting from the speakers' platform in the Forum: have you forgotten what these things are? 'But people care about them.' So you'll be a fool too?

He ends with a definition: being 'fortunate' means giving yourself a good fortune, and good fortune is a good character, good emotions, good actions.

Today: comfort someone over a loss without pretending it's bigger than it is.
meditations-6.1:
The substance of the universe is obedient and pliable, Marcus says, and the reason that governs it has no motive to do evil. It has no malice, does no harm, and nothing is harmed by it. Everything is made and completed according to that reason.

It's the Stoic picture of a benign cosmos: not a hostile or indifferent place, but one shaped by a reason that intends no ill. Whatever you think of that, it shapes how Marcus approaches everything else.

Today: notice one way the world around you works quietly in your favor.
meditations-6.2:
It shouldn't matter to you, Marcus says, whether you're cold or warm, sleepy or rested, criticized or praised, dying or doing something else, as long as you're doing your duty. Dying is just one of the acts of life, and it's enough to do it well too.

The last thought is striking: death isn't outside life but one more thing you do, and can do well or badly. The same principle applies to everything: focus on the task, not the conditions.

Today: do your work well regardless of how you feel while doing it.
enchiridion-15:
Behave in life as at a banquet, Epictetus says. Is something passed to you? Reach out and take a modest share. Has it passed you by? Don't grab for it. Hasn't it reached you yet? Don't strain toward it; wait until it comes. Do this with children, spouse, office and wealth, and one day you'll be worthy to dine with the gods.

And if you don't even take what's offered, but can let it go, you'll be worthy not only to dine with the gods but to rule with them. That's how Diogenes and Heraclitus came to be called divine.

It's a gracious model for desire: take your share calmly, don't grab, don't pine.

Today: let one good thing come to you in its own time, without grasping.
meditations-6.3:
Look inward, Marcus says. Don't let the true nature or value of anything escape you.

It's a two-part instruction. 'Look within' sends attention to your own judgments rather than to appearances. And 'don't miss the real quality or worth' asks you to see through surfaces to what things actually are. Both are about seeing clearly instead of reacting to how things look.

Today: look past the surface of one thing that impresses or bothers you.
meditations-6.4:
Everything that exists will soon change, Marcus says. It will either turn to vapor, if all matter is one, or scatter.

The either-or reflects his habit of not insisting on one theory of the universe. Whether Stoic physics or atomism is right, the practical conclusion is the same: everything is temporary, and that's how the world works.

Today: let one temporary thing be temporary without fighting it.
meditations-6.5:
The governing reason knows its own disposition, Marcus says: what it's doing and what material it's working on.

This is about self-awareness. A mind working well knows its own state, its own actions and its circumstances. It isn't operating blindly. That knowledge is what makes it possible to act deliberately instead of reactively.

Today: pause once and ask: what state am I in, what am I doing, and what am I working with?
meditations-6.6:
'The best revenge is not to become like the one who wronged you.'

It's one of Marcus's most quoted lines. Retaliation tends to make you resemble the person you resent: petty, cruel or dishonest in return. Refusing to be changed by them is both the higher road and, in a sense, the real victory.

Today: if someone treats you badly, respond in a way they wouldn't.
meditations-6.7:
Take pleasure in one thing and rest in it, Marcus says: moving from one act of service to the next, with God in mind.

For Marcus, the satisfaction of a good life isn't found in rest or reward but in the flow of doing good: one helpful act leading to the next. That chain of useful work, done mindfully, is itself the pleasure.

Today: after finishing one helpful thing, move straight to the next.
meditations-6.8:
The ruling faculty rouses and steers itself, Marcus says. It makes itself what it is and what it wants to be, and it makes everything that happens appear to it as it chooses.

This is the Stoic claim about autonomy. Your mind shapes both itself and how events appear to it. You can't always choose what happens, but you can choose what it looks like to you, by the judgments you make.

Today: pick one event and deliberately choose how to see it.
meditations-6.9:
Everything is accomplished in line with the nature of the universe, Marcus says. Not according to some other nature outside it, or hidden within it, or separate from it.

It's a compact statement of Stoic monism: there's one nature and one order, and everything happens within it. There's no rival power or separate realm working against it.

The practical upshot is acceptance: what happens isn't an intrusion from outside the order, but part of it.

Today: treat one unexpected event as part of the normal order of things.
meditations-6.10:
Either the universe is a jumble and scattering, Marcus says, or it's unity, order and providence. If it's a jumble, why would I want to stay in such chaos? Why care about anything except how I'll turn to earth? Why be upset, since I'll be scattered whatever I do?

But if there's order, I revere it, I stand firm, and I trust the one who governs.

He often uses this either-or. Both branches lead to calm: either nothing matters enough to disturb you, or everything is in good hands.

Today: when worried, ask whether worrying helps under either view.
meditations-6.11:
When circumstances force you to be shaken, Marcus says, come back to yourself quickly, and don't stay out of tune longer than you must. You'll master the harmony by returning to it constantly.

The music image is helpful. No one stays perfectly in tune; the skill is in noticing and coming back. The more often you return, the easier it becomes.

Today: when you get rattled, see how quickly you can return to calm.
enchiridion-16:
When you see someone weeping in grief, Epictetus says, because their child has gone abroad or they've had a loss, don't be swept away by the apparent evil. Remember: what's hurting them isn't the event, since someone else might not be hurt by it, but their view of it.

As far as words go, though, don't hesitate to sympathize, and if it helps, even to groan with them. But be careful not to groan inwardly as well.

It's a careful balance: outward compassion without inward collapse. You can comfort someone without adopting their judgment that it's a catastrophe.

Today: comfort someone fully, while keeping your own calm inside.
meditations-6.12:
If you had both a stepmother and a mother, Marcus says, you'd treat the stepmother dutifully, but you'd keep going back to your mother. Let the imperial court be your stepmother and philosophy your mother. Go back to philosophy often and rest in her; she makes court life bearable for you, and you bearable at court.

It's a candid note from an emperor about life among courtiers, politics and flattery. Philosophy is his home base.

Today: go back to whatever steadies you, even for a few minutes.
meditations-6.13:
When you look at a fine meal, Marcus says, you can see it as a dead fish, a dead bird, a dead pig. Expensive Falernian wine is just grape juice. A purple robe is sheep's wool dyed with shellfish blood. Such views cut through to what things really are.

Do this all through life, especially with things that seem most impressive. Strip away the grand words around them. Appearances are a great deceiver of reason, and they fool you most when you're sure you're busy with something important.

He ends by pointing to an anecdote about the Cynic Crates and Xenocrates that hasn't survived.

Today: describe one thing you prize in deliberately plain terms.
meditations-6.14:
Marcus ranks what people admire. Most admire things held together by mere structure: stones, wood, vines and olives. Slightly more thoughtful people admire living things: flocks and herds. More educated people admire things with a rational soul, but narrowly, for being skilled, or for owning many slaves.

But someone who values the rational, social soul itself cares for nothing else. Above all they keep their own mind reasonable and community-minded, and work with others who share that aim.

The ladder is a way of asking what you really value: possessions, living things, skill, or character itself.

Today: notice which rung of his ladder your admiration usually sits on.
meditations-6.15:
Some things are rushing into existence, Marcus says, others rushing out, and part of what is arriving has already gone. Change constantly renews the world. In such a stream, what's worth prizing? It would be like falling in love with a sparrow flying past, already out of sight.

Life itself is like that, like breathing in and out. You received your breath at birth, 'yesterday or the day before', and you'll give it back.

The sparrow image is gentle. It isn't that nothing is lovely, but that clinging to passing things is a recipe for grief.

Today: enjoy one passing thing without trying to hold on to it.
meditations-6.16:
What's worth valuing? Marcus asks. Not breathing, like plants and animals; not receiving impressions or being jerked by desires; not herding together or eating. Not applause either; praise from crowds is just tongues clapping.

What's left? To act and restrain yourself in line with your nature, which is the aim of every craft and of all education. If you value that, you'll stop valuing other things.

If you don't, you'll never be free or self-sufficient. You'll envy and suspect anyone who could take what you prize, and plot against those who have it. But honoring your own mind makes you content with yourself, at peace with others, and in harmony with the gods.

Today: let go of one thing you're anxious to keep, and notice how much freer you feel.
meditations-6.17:
Above, below and all around, Marcus says, the elements are in motion. But virtue's movement isn't among them. It's something more divine, traveling a path hardly noticed, and it goes happily on its way.

It's a quiet image: while everything visible churns, goodness moves by a different, less conspicuous route. You can't always see it, but it proceeds.

Today: do one good thing quietly, without needing it to be seen.
meditations-6.18:
How strange people are, Marcus says. They won't praise those living alongside them, but they long to be praised by future generations they've never met and never will. That's like being upset that people born before you didn't praise you.

The comparison exposes the oddness of craving posthumous fame. Future people are as remote from you as past ones; their praise is no more yours to have.

Today: praise someone living around you, instead of hoping to be praised later.
meditations-6.19:
If something is hard for you, Marcus says, don't assume it's impossible for a human being. But if something is possible for humans and fits human nature, assume you can do it too.

It's encouragement grounded in logic. Your difficulty isn't proof of impossibility, and others' achievements show what is possible. If someone has managed it, it's within human reach, including yours.

Today: try something you've assumed is beyond you, because someone else has done it.
meditations-6.20:
In wrestling practice, Marcus says, someone might scratch you or butt your head. We don't sulk, take offense or treat them as treacherous afterwards. We keep an eye on them, not as an enemy or with suspicion, but just stay out of their way.

Behave like that in the rest of life. Overlook a lot in people who are like sparring partners. You can step aside without suspicion or hatred.

It's a practical model for dealing with difficult people: wary but not hostile, careful but not bitter.

Today: treat one difficult person like a sparring partner rather than an enemy.
enchiridion-17:
Remember you're an actor in a play, Epictetus says, of the kind the author chooses: short if he wants it short, long if long. If he wants you to play a poor man, a disabled man, a ruler or a private citizen, play it well. Your job is to play the part you're given well; choosing it belongs to someone else.

It's one of the most freeing ideas in Stoicism. You don't pick your role, but you control how well you perform it. That's where your dignity lies.

Today: play your role, whatever it is today, as well as you can.
meditations-6.21:
If anyone can show me I'm thinking or acting wrongly, Marcus says, I'll gladly change. I'm looking for the truth, and no one was ever harmed by the truth. The person harmed is the one who persists in error and ignorance.

From a Roman emperor, the willingness to be corrected is striking. He frames correction not as a loss of face but as a gain: truth never hurts you, ignorance does.

Today: invite one person to tell you where you might be wrong.
meditations-6.22:
I do my duty, Marcus says. Other things don't bother me, because they're either lifeless, or without reason, or people who've wandered and don't know the way.

It's a sorting device. Things are neutral; animals don't reason; people who behave badly are lost rather than malicious. None of these deserves to disturb you while you're doing your own part.

Today: focus on your own duty and let three other things go.
meditations-6.23:
Toward animals and things that lack reason, Marcus says, use them generously and freely, since you have reason and they don't. Toward people, since they have reason, act in a spirit of fellowship. And always call on the gods, without fretting about how long you'll get to do this; even three hours lived that way is enough.

The last line is the gem: a good life isn't measured in length. A short stretch lived well is complete.

Today: spend three hours living as well as you know how.
meditations-6.24:
Alexander the Great and his groom ended in the same state, Marcus says. Either both were taken back into the creative principles of the universe, or both were scattered among atoms.

It's a classic leveler. The conqueror of the known world and his humble servant met the same end. Whatever you think happens after death, it happens equally to the great and the ordinary.

Today: treat someone of lower status exactly as you'd treat someone of higher status.
meditations-6.25:
Think how many things happen in each of us at the same instant, Marcus says, in the body and the mind. Then you won't be surprised that far more, indeed everything that comes to be, exists at once in the one great whole we call the cosmos.

It's a way of grasping the scale of reality. Even your own body is busy with countless processes at any moment; the universe is that, multiplied beyond imagining.

Today: take a moment to notice how much is going on in you right now without your effort.
meditations-6.26:
If someone asked you to spell the name 'Antoninus', Marcus says, would you shout each letter? If they got angry, would you get angry too? Wouldn't you just calmly go through the letters one by one?

Life is like that. Every duty is made of parts. Attend to them, and without being rattled or getting angry at angry people, go on and finish what's in front of you.

The spelling image is wonderfully ordinary. Big tasks become manageable when you take them letter by letter.

Today: break one daunting task into its smallest parts and do the first one calmly.
meditations-6.27:
How cruel it is, Marcus says, not to let people pursue what seems good and useful to them. Yet in a way that's what you do when you're annoyed at their wrongdoing. They're drawn to things because they think those things are good for them. They're mistaken. So teach them and show them, without anger.

The insight is compassionate. People who do wrong usually think they're doing something good. Anger treats them as villains; teaching treats them as people who are wrong.

Today: when someone errs, assume they thought they were doing something good.
meditations-6.28:
Death, Marcus says, is the end of sense impressions, of desire jerking us like puppets, of restless thought, and of serving the body.

Put this way, death sounds almost like rest. He doesn't deny its weight, but he lists what it relieves us of: constant stimulation, compulsion, mental churn and bodily demands. It's meant to make death less fearsome.

Today: notice one of those four burdens, and lighten it a little while you're alive.
meditations-6.29:
It's shameful, Marcus says, for the soul to give up in life before the body does.

The body may be tired, ill or ageing, but it keeps going. For the mind to quit earlier, through discouragement, apathy or despair, is to fail in the one area where you have the most control.

Today: when you feel like giving up mentally, notice that your body is still going.
meditations-6.30:
'Take care not to be turned into a Caesar, not to be dyed purple by it; it happens.' Marcus warns himself against being changed by power. Stay simple, good, pure, serious, unaffected, just, devout, kind, affectionate and energetic in your duties. Life is short; its one harvest is a good character and helpful actions.

Then he holds up his adoptive father Antoninus Pius as the model: steady, calm, uninterested in fame, careful to understand everything before acting, patient with unfair critics, never hurried, deaf to gossip, content with little, hardworking, loyal in friendship, open to disagreement, glad to be shown better, devout without superstition.

Imitate all this, he says, so you'll have as clear a conscience at the end as he did.

Today: pick one quality of a person you admire, and practice it.
enchiridion-18:
When a raven croaks an unlucky omen, Epictetus says, don't be carried away. Say, 'Nothing is foretold to me, only to my little body, property, reputation, children or spouse. For me every omen is lucky if I want it to be, because whatever happens, it's up to me to benefit from it.'

Ancient people took omens seriously. Epictetus says that whatever an omen predicts concerns only externals. Your response is yours, and any event can be turned to good use.

Today: take one bad sign and decide how you'll benefit from whatever follows.
meditations-6.31:
Come back to your senses, Marcus says. Wake yourself, and when you realize it was only dreams that troubled you, look at what's around you now the way you looked at those dreams.

It's a striking suggestion. When we wake from a bad dream we feel relief that it wasn't real. Marcus asks us to see many of our waking worries the same way: as impressions, not facts.

Today: look at one worry as if it were a dream you've just woken from.
meditations-6.32:
I'm made of a small body and a soul, Marcus says. To the body everything is indifferent, since it can't judge. To the mind, the only things that aren't indifferent are its own activities, and those are in its power. Even then, only present activity counts; past and future thinking is, for now, indifferent too.

This narrows your real concerns to a sharp point: what your mind is doing right now. Not what happened to you, not what you did yesterday, not what you might do tomorrow.

Today: when you dwell on the past or future, bring attention back to what your mind is doing now.
meditations-6.33:
Neither the hand's work nor the foot's is against nature, Marcus says, as long as each does its own job. Likewise, work isn't against a person's nature as long as it's the work proper to a human being. And if it isn't against your nature, it isn't bad for you.

It's a reassurance about effort. Labor, even hard labor, isn't a misfortune in itself. What matters is whether it's the right kind of work for a reasoning, social being.

Today: do one hard task as if it were exactly the work you were made for.
meditations-6.34:
A single bitter observation: how many pleasures have been enjoyed by robbers, parricides and tyrants.

Marcus's point is that pleasure can't be what makes a life good, because the worst people have plenty of it. If criminals and tyrants can enjoy something fully, then enjoying it proves nothing about the worth of your life.

Today: ask whether one pleasure you value is something a bad person could enjoy just as much.
meditations-6.35:
Look at craftsmen, Marcus says. They'll accommodate customers who know nothing of their trade up to a point, but they hold firmly to the principles of their craft and won't abandon them. Isn't it strange that an architect or a doctor respects the rules of their art more than a person respects their own reason, which they share with the gods?

The comparison is pointed. We admire professionals who refuse to cut corners. Why are we so willing to compromise on the principles of living well?

Today: hold to one principle as firmly as a good craftsman holds to their standards.
meditations-6.36:
Asia and Europe are corners of the universe, Marcus says; the whole sea a drop; Mount Athos a clod of earth; all present time a point in eternity. Everything is small, changeable, perishable.

And everything comes from the same governing source, directly or as a consequence. Even a lion's gaping jaws, poison, thorns and mud are by-products of something grand and beautiful. Don't think they come from a different source than what you revere.

The passage pairs humility about scale with acceptance of the unpleasant: both belong to the same whole.

Today: see one unpleasant thing as part of the same world as the things you love.
meditations-6.37:
Whoever has seen the present has seen everything, Marcus says: everything that has happened from all eternity and everything that will happen forever. All things are of one kind and one form.

It's a striking claim of sameness. Human life repeats its patterns: ambition, love, conflict, grief. Understanding today well is a way of understanding all of history.

Today: notice one situation that people have faced in exactly this form for thousands of years.
meditations-6.38:
Often think about how everything in the universe is connected, Marcus says. All things are intertwined and, in a way, friendly to one another, because one follows another in order through shared movement, shared breath and the unity of substance.

The Stoics called this sympathy: everything affects everything else. It's a view of the world as a web of relationships rather than a collection of separate objects.

Today: trace how one thing you depend on connects to many people and things you never see.
meditations-6.39:
Adapt yourself to the circumstances your lot has been cast in, Marcus says, and love the people you've been given to live among, but love them genuinely.

The last words matter. It's easy to tolerate the people around you, or to perform affection for them. Marcus asks for real love toward the specific, imperfect people you actually share life with.

Today: do one genuinely kind thing for someone you live or work with.
enchiridion-19:
You can be unbeatable, Epictetus says, if you never enter a contest you can't win, meaning a contest over things outside your control. So when you see someone with honors, power or esteem, don't be dazzled and call them happy. If the good lies in what's in our power, there's no room for envy or rivalry.

Don't want to be a general, a senator or a consul. Want to be free. And the only way there is to stop caring about what isn't in your power.

It's a clever reframe of competition: choose games where victory is always available.

Today: stop competing in one area where you don't control the outcome.
meditations-6.40:
Every tool or vessel, Marcus says, is fine if it does what it was made for, even though its maker is absent. But in natural things, the power that made them stays within them. So it's all the more fitting to revere that power, and to recognize that living by its will keeps everything in you in line with intelligence, as it does in the universe.

The contrast is between a made object and a living thing. Your own nature carries its maker's design inside it. Following that design is following the intelligence that shaped you.

Today: treat your own better instincts as a design worth following.
meditations-6.41:
If you treat things outside your control as good or bad for you, Marcus says, then when you lose a good or suffer a bad, you'll inevitably blame the gods and resent the people responsible, or the people you suspect. Much injustice comes from this.

But if you count only what's in your control as good or bad, you'll have no reason to blame God or be hostile to anyone.

This is the Stoic case for indifference to externals: it isn't coldness, but a way of not poisoning your relationships with resentment.

Today: when you're about to blame someone, ask whether it's for something that really determines your good.
meditations-6.42:
We're all working toward one end, Marcus says: some knowingly, others unaware, like sleepers who, as Heraclitus said, are still workers in the universe. Even people who complain about events or try to obstruct them contribute; the universe needs them too.

So the question is what kind of worker you'll be. The governor of all things will make good use of you either way. But don't be like the cheap, silly line in a play that Chrysippus described: technically part of the whole, but the worst part.

Today: ask whether you're cooperating with what happens or just complaining about it.
meditations-6.43:
Does the sun try to do the rain's job? Marcus asks. Does the god of healing try to do the earth's job of bearing fruit? And the stars: aren't they all different, yet working together to the same end?

It's a picture of cooperation through difference. Everyone has their own role, and the whole works because each part does its own thing well rather than trying to do everyone else's.

Today: do your own role well instead of envying or second-guessing someone else's.
meditations-6.44:
Marcus reasons through providence. If the gods have planned for me, they've planned well; it's hard to imagine a god without foresight, and why would they want to harm me? If they haven't planned for me individually, they've planned for the whole, and I should accept what follows from that. If they plan nothing at all, which it's wrong to believe, then I can still plan for myself and ask what's useful.

And what's useful is what fits my nature, which is rational and social. 'As Antoninus, my city and country is Rome; as a human being, it's the world.' What benefits those communities is what benefits me.

Today: make one choice by asking what helps your community, not just yourself.
meditations-6.45:
Whatever happens to anyone serves the good of the whole, Marcus says, and that should be enough. But you'll also notice that what genuinely benefits one person generally benefits others too.

He adds a qualification: here 'benefit' is used in the ordinary sense, for things neither truly good nor bad, like health and money. The deeper point is that real advantage isn't zero-sum. What's good for one is rarely bad for all.

Today: look for a choice that benefits you and someone else at the same time.
meditations-6.46:
At the amphitheater, Marcus says, seeing the same thing over and over, all alike, makes the show tedious. Life is like that: everything above and below is the same, from the same source. How long then?

It's a weary note. Marcus had to attend the public games and found them dull. He applies the same feeling to life's repetitions. The final question, 'how long?', is less despair than a reminder that the show isn't worth clinging to.

Today: notice one repetitive part of your life and ask whether it deserves the importance you give it.
meditations-6.47:
Think constantly, Marcus says, that people of every kind, every pursuit and every nation are dead, down to obscure names like Philistion, Phoebus and Origanion. Then think of the great: orators, philosophers like Heraclitus, Pythagoras and Socrates, ancient heroes, generals and tyrants; brilliant minds like Eudoxus, Hipparchus and Archimedes; and mockers of human life like the satirist Menippus. All long in the dust.

What harm is that to them, or to the forgotten? One thing is worth a great deal: living truthfully and justly, kind even to liars and the unjust.

Today: be kind to someone who doesn't deserve it.
meditations-6.48:
When you want to cheer yourself up, Marcus says, think of the good qualities of the people around you: one person's energy, another's modesty, another's generosity. Nothing delights like seeing virtues in the people you live with, as many as possible. So keep them in view.

It's a lovely, practical tip. Instead of dwelling on people's faults, deliberately catalog their strengths. It improves your mood and your relationships at once.

Today: list one good quality in three people you'll see.
enchiridion-20:
It isn't the person who insults or hits you who wrongs you, Epictetus says, but your judgment that they're insulting you. When someone provokes you, know that your own opinion has provoked you. So first, try not to be swept away by appearances. If you can buy yourself time and a pause, you'll find it easier to control yourself.

The practical tip at the end is gold: delay. The heat of a reaction fades with even a short pause.

Today: when provoked, wait before responding.
meditations-6.49:
You're not upset that you weigh only so many pounds and not three hundred, Marcus says. So don't be upset that you'll live only so many years and not more. Be as content with your allotted time as with your allotted body.

The comparison is playful but pointed. We accept many limits without complaint. Lifespan is just another one, and resenting it makes as little sense as resenting your height.

Today: accept one personal limit without wishing it were different.
meditations-6.50:
Try to persuade people, Marcus says, but act even against their will when justice requires it. If someone blocks you by force, accept it calmly, and use the obstacle to practice a different virtue.

Remember that you acted with a reservation: you never wanted the impossible. What did you want? To make the effort. And you achieved that, even if the result didn't happen.

This is the Stoic 'reserve clause': aim at outcomes, but locate your success in the effort. That keeps you active without making you hostage to results.

Today: commit to one effort, and count it as success whatever the outcome.
meditations-6.51:
Someone who loves fame thinks other people's actions are his good, Marcus says. Someone who loves pleasure thinks his sensations are his good. But someone with understanding thinks his own actions are his good.

It's a neat diagnosis of where people locate their happiness: in others' opinions, in their own feelings, or in their own conduct. Only the last is really yours to control.

Today: judge your day by your actions, not by others' reactions or your own moods.
meditations-6.52:
It's in our power to have no opinion about a thing, Marcus says, and not be disturbed. Things themselves have no power to form our judgments.

This is one of the quietest and most useful Stoic moves: sometimes you don't need to decide whether something is good or bad at all. You can simply let it be, unjudged, and it loses its grip on you.

Today: let one thing pass without forming an opinion about it.
meditations-6.53:
Train yourself to listen carefully to what others say, Marcus says, and as far as possible, get inside the speaker's mind.

Real listening isn't waiting for your turn. It's trying to understand what the other person means and why. It's harder than it sounds, and it changes conversations.

Today: in one conversation, try to understand the other person's view well enough to state it back to them.
meditations-6.54:
'What isn't good for the hive isn't good for the bee.'

It's one of Marcus's most compact statements of Stoic social ethics. Your good and the common good aren't opposed. Something that harms the community can't truly benefit you, however it looks in the short term.

Today: before one decision, ask whether it's good for the hive as well as the bee.
meditations-6.55:
If sailors abused their helmsman, Marcus asks, or patients their doctor, who else would they listen to? And how could the helmsman keep the ship safe, or the doctor restore health?

It's a comment on attacking the people whose job is to help us. Contempt for expertise or leadership doesn't make you safer. Coming from an emperor, it may also reflect his own frustrations with critics.

Today: give one person who's trying to help you the benefit of the doubt.
meditations-6.56:
How many of those who came into the world with me have already left it.

A quiet, sobering line. Marcus counts the peers he's outlived. It isn't despair, but a reminder of how short and uncertain life is, and an implicit nudge to use what's left well.

Today: think of one person you've lost, and honor them by living one hour well.
meditations-6.57:
To someone with jaundice, honey tastes bitter, Marcus says. To someone bitten by a rabid dog, water is terrifying. To small children, a ball is a wonderful thing. So why am I angry? Do I think a false opinion has less power than bile in the jaundiced or poison in someone bitten?

The point is compassion through understanding. People's mistaken views shape what they see as surely as illness shapes taste. Being angry at them is like being angry at a fever.

Today: when someone sees things wrongly, treat it as a condition, not a crime.
meditations-6.58:
No one can stop you living according to the reason of your own nature, Marcus says, and nothing will happen to you against the reason of the universe.

It's a two-sided reassurance. Your freedom to act well can't be taken away. And whatever happens to you fits the larger order. Between them, there's nothing to fear and nothing that can stop you.

Today: act on your best judgment in one situation where you've been holding back.
enchiridion-21:
Keep death and exile, and everything that seems terrible, before your eyes every day, Epictetus says, but death above all. Then you'll never have a mean thought or want anything too much.

Regular reflection on loss and mortality isn't morbid. It shrinks petty worries and excessive cravings, and puts what matters back in focus.

Today: spend a moment remembering that life is finite, and let one small worry go.
meditations-6.59:
What kind of people do others try to please, Marcus asks, for what ends, and by what means? And how quickly time covers everything, and how much it has already covered.

The questions expose people-pleasing. Often we contort ourselves for approval from people whose judgment we don't respect, for goals we don't value, by means we're not proud of. And all of it will soon be forgotten.

Today: notice one person you're trying to please, and ask why.
meditations-7.1:
What is wickedness? Marcus asks. It's what you've seen many times. And whenever anything happens, remember: you've seen this before. Everywhere you'll find the same things that fill the histories of ancient times, recent times and today, and fill cities and houses now. Nothing is new; everything is familiar and short-lived.

It's a way of draining the shock out of bad behavior and bad news. Human failings repeat themselves; recognizing that makes them less disturbing and easier to deal with calmly.

Today: when something outrages you, remind yourself it has happened countless times before.
meditations-7.2:
How can your principles die, Marcus asks, unless the thoughts that keep them alive go out? But you can always fan those thoughts back into flame. I can hold the opinion I ought to hold about anything. If I can, why am I disturbed? Things outside my mind have no hold on it.

Recovering your life is in your power: look at things again as you used to. That's the recovery.

It's an encouraging passage for anyone who feels they've lost their way. Principles fade with neglect, but they can be relit.

Today: reread one idea that once helped you, and let it matter again.
meditations-7.3:
Marcus lists life's busy theater: empty shows, stage plays, flocks and herds, mock spear fights, a bone thrown to puppies, crumbs tossed into fishponds, ants hauling loads, frightened mice scurrying, puppets on strings.

In the middle of all this, he says, your job is to be good-humored, not superior, while understanding that each person is worth exactly as much as the things they busy themselves about.

It's a gentle balance: see the comedy of human striving without sneering at it, and choose your own pursuits carefully, because they measure you.

Today: look at what you're busy with, and ask what it says about your worth.
meditations-7.4:
In conversation, Marcus says, pay attention to what's said; in action, pay attention to what's done. With words, see immediately what they're aiming at; with actions, watch carefully what they mean.

It's a call for alertness. Words have purposes behind them, and actions have meanings beyond what they look like. Paying close attention to both is how you understand people and situations accurately.

Today: in one conversation, listen for what the other person is aiming at, not just what they say.
meditations-7.5:
Is my understanding up to this task? Marcus asks. If so, I use it as a tool nature gave me. If not, I either step aside for someone better suited, unless there's a reason not to, or I do it as best I can with help from someone who can do what's needed for the common good.

Whatever I do, alone or with others, should aim only at what is useful and fitting for the community.

It's a refreshingly practical attitude from a ruler: no ego about doing everything himself, just a focus on getting it done well.

Today: ask for help with one thing someone else could do better.
meditations-7.6:
How many who were celebrated have been forgotten, Marcus says, and how many who celebrated others are long dead.

Both sides of fame vanish: the famous and the people who made them famous. It's a short line that dissolves the appeal of reputation. Neither praising nor being praised lasts.

Today: do one thing for its own value, not for anyone's notice.
meditations-7.7:
Don't be ashamed to be helped, Marcus says. Your job is to do your duty, like a soldier storming a wall. What if you're lame and can't climb the battlements alone, but can with a comrade's help?

It's a needed corrective to Stoic self-reliance. Accepting help isn't weakness; it's how you complete the task. Pride that refuses help can leave the duty undone.

Today: accept help with something you'd usually insist on doing alone.
meditations-7.8:
Don't let the future disturb you, Marcus says. You'll meet it, if you must, with the same reason you use for the present.

It's simple and steadying. Anxiety about the future assumes you'll face it unequipped. But you'll bring the same mind you have now, the one that's handling today. That's enough.

Today: when you worry about something ahead, remember you'll meet it with the same mind that's handling today.
enchiridion-22:
If you're serious about philosophy, Epictetus says, expect to be laughed at. People will say, 'Look, he's suddenly a philosopher,' and 'Where did that superior look come from?'

Don't put on a superior look. But hold steadily to what seems best, as though God had posted you there. If you persist, the people who laughed will come to admire you. If you give in, you'll be laughed at twice.

It's encouragement for anyone trying to change in public: expect mockery, stay humble, and don't quit.

Today: keep doing one good habit even if someone teases you for it.
meditations-7.9:
Everything is interwoven, Marcus says, and the bond is sacred; almost nothing is unconnected. All things are arranged together to form one ordered universe. There is one universe made of everything, one god pervading everything, one substance, one law, one reason shared by all thinking beings, and one truth.

It's one of his fullest statements of Stoic unity. Everything belongs to a single whole, and reason is what all humans have in common.

Today: treat one disagreement as a difference within a shared reason, not a clash of strangers.
meditations-7.10:
Everything material soon disappears into the whole, Marcus says; everything formative is soon taken back into universal reason; and the memory of everything is soon overwhelmed by time.

Three kinds of disappearance: matter, form and memory. Everything you are and do will dissolve in one of these ways. It's meant not to depress but to loosen your grip.

Today: hold one thing more lightly, knowing it's temporary.
meditations-7.11:
For a rational being, Marcus says, acting according to nature and acting according to reason are the same thing.

This is a central Stoic idea. Our nature is to be reasonable, so 'natural' doesn't mean following impulses like an animal. It means using reason well. Acting thoughtfully isn't going against your nature; it's fulfilling it.

Today: when an impulse feels 'natural', ask whether it's reasonable too.
meditations-7.12:
'Be upright, or be made upright.'

The shortest passage in the book, at seven words. Marcus is saying you can either stand straight by your own effort, or be straightened by others, by correction, consequences or circumstances. Better to do it yourself.

Today: correct one thing in yourself before someone else has to.
meditations-7.13:
Just as limbs belong to one body, Marcus says, rational beings, though separate, are made to work together. You'll feel this more if you tell yourself, 'I am a limb of the body of rational beings.'

He then makes a pun that works in Greek: if you only call yourself a 'part' (meros) rather than a 'limb' (melos), changing one letter, you don't yet love people from the heart. Kindness doesn't yet delight you for its own sake; you do it out of duty, not as doing good to yourself.

The difference is between belonging and merely being included.

Today: help someone because it's good for you too, not just because you should.
meditations-7.14:
Let whatever will fall on the parts of me that can feel it, Marcus says. Those parts can complain if they like. But unless I judge that what happened is bad, I'm not harmed, and it's in my power not to judge it so.

This is classic Stoicism: the body may suffer, but the self isn't harmed unless it agrees that it has been. That agreement is the one thing you control.

Today: when something hurts, separate the sensation from the verdict.
meditations-7.15:
Whatever anyone does or says, Marcus says, I must be good, just as gold, an emerald or purple dye would always say: whatever anyone does or says, I must be an emerald and keep my color.

It's a lovely image of integrity. An emerald doesn't stop being green because someone insults it. Your character shouldn't change color depending on how others behave.

Today: keep your character steady with one person who usually provokes you.
meditations-7.16:
The ruling faculty doesn't disturb itself, Marcus says. It doesn't frighten itself or cause itself pain. If someone else can frighten or hurt it, let them try. It won't turn itself that way by its own judgment.

Let the body take care of itself and complain if it suffers. But the part that can feel fear and pain, and judges them, will suffer nothing unless it chooses to. It needs nothing unless it invents a need, so it stays calm and unobstructed, as long as it doesn't disturb or obstruct itself.

The theme is that your mind is its own worst threat and best protector.

Today: notice when you're frightening yourself with your own thoughts.
meditations-7.17:
In Greek, the word for happiness, eudaimonia, literally means having a good daemon, a good inner spirit. Marcus plays on that. So what are you doing here, imagination? Go away, by the gods, the way you came. I don't want you. You've come in your old habit. I'm not angry with you; just leave.

It's a gentle way of handling an unwanted thought: not fighting it, just politely dismissing it.

Today: when a familiar unhelpful thought shows up, tell it calmly to go.
enchiridion-23:
If you ever turn toward outward things to please someone, Epictetus says, know that you've wrecked your plan of life. Be content in everything with being a philosopher. And if you want to seem one to someone, seem one to yourself; that's enough.

The pull to perform for others is constant. Epictetus says your own honest assessment should be the audience that matters.

Today: do one good thing for your own sake, not for anyone watching.
meditations-7.18:
Is anyone afraid of change? Marcus asks. What can happen without it? What's more natural to the universe? Can you have a hot bath unless the firewood changes? Can you eat unless food changes? Can anything useful be done without change? So don't you see that your own change is just the same, and just as necessary to nature?

The examples are deliberately homely. We welcome change constantly when it serves us. Fearing it in ourselves, including ageing and death, is inconsistent.

Today: notice three useful changes you rely on without thinking.
meditations-7.19:
All bodies are swept through the universe as through a raging torrent, Marcus says, united with the whole and cooperating with it like the parts of our body. How many a Chrysippus, a Socrates, an Epictetus has time already swallowed!

He names three of the philosophers he most admired. Even they were carried off. Apply the same thought to every person and thing.

It's humbling: not even wisdom exempts anyone from the current. But it also places the great alongside the ordinary, all part of the same stream.

Today: remember someone you admire who is gone, and carry forward one thing they taught.
meditations-7.20:
Only one thing troubles me, Marcus says: that I might do something human nature doesn't allow, or in a way it doesn't allow, or at a time it doesn't allow.

It's a remarkable statement of focus. Not illness, criticism or loss, but only the possibility of acting wrongly. And he breaks wrongness into three: what you do, how you do it, and when.

Today: before one action, check all three: is it right, done rightly, and at the right time?
meditations-7.21:
Soon you'll have forgotten everything, Marcus says, and soon everyone will have forgotten you.

It's one of his starkest lines on mortality. Both directions of memory fade: yours of the world, and the world's of you. Taken calmly, it frees you from living for remembrance and points you back to living well now.

Today: do one thing because it's right, not because anyone will remember it.
meditations-7.22:
It's distinctively human, Marcus says, to love even those who do wrong. That becomes possible when you remember they're your kin, that they act out of ignorance and not on purpose, that you'll both be dead soon, and above all that they haven't harmed you, because they haven't made your mind worse than before.

It's a demanding ideal, but he gives practical steps: see them as family, assume ignorance, remember mortality, and remember your character is untouched.

Today: apply one of those four thoughts to someone who has wronged you.
meditations-7.23:
Nature takes the universal substance like wax, Marcus says, and moulds a horse; then breaks it up and uses the material for a tree, then a person, then something else. Each lasts only briefly. But being broken up is no hardship for the vessel, any more than being put together was.

The wax image is vivid and calming. We're temporary shapes in a material that keeps being reworked. Being unmade is no more a tragedy than being made.

Today: think of something you've lost as returned material rather than destroyed.
meditations-7.24:
A scowling face is unnatural, Marcus says. When it's worn often, all attractiveness dies away until it can't be relit. Conclude from this that it's contrary to reason. And if even the awareness of doing wrong leaves us, what reason is left for living?

He's noticing that habitual sourness shapes us: it shows in the face, and eventually it becomes us. The deeper worry is losing the ability to notice our own faults.

Today: notice your facial expression a few times, and soften it.
meditations-7.25:
The nature that governs the whole will soon change everything you see, Marcus says. Out of its substance it will make other things, and from those still others, so that the world is always new.

It's a quietly optimistic view of change. Things don't just end; they're remade. Endings are the price of a world that stays fresh.

Today: look at one ending in your life as making room for something new.
meditations-7.26:
When someone wrongs you, Marcus says, immediately ask what idea of good and bad led them to do it. Once you see that, you'll pity them rather than be shocked or angry. Either you share their idea of what's good, or something like it, and should forgive them. Or you don't think such things are good or bad, and you'll find it easier to be kind to someone who's mistaken.

It's an exercise in understanding before judging. Most wrongs come from mistaken values, not pure malice.

Today: when someone frustrates you, ask what they thought they were gaining.
meditations-7.27:
Don't think so much about what you lack as about what you have, Marcus says. Of what you have, pick the best, and think how eagerly you'd seek them if you didn't have them. But be careful not to become so attached that you'd be devastated to lose them.

It's a balanced gratitude exercise: appreciate what you have by imagining its absence, but hold it loosely enough that losing it won't break you.

Today: pick one thing you have, imagine not having it, then hold it a little more lightly.
enchiridion-24:
Don't worry, Epictetus says, that you'll live without honor and be a nobody. If dishonor were an evil, no one else could inflict it on you, any more than they could make you shameful. You should be somebody only where it's in your power, and there you can matter enormously.

'But my friends won't get help from me.' You mean money or Roman citizenship? Those were never in your power to give. 'Then get them so we can share.' If I can do it while keeping my honor, show me how. But if you'd have me lose my real good so you can gain something that isn't good, that's foolish. Wouldn't you rather have a faithful friend than money?

And your country? It doesn't need porticoes and baths from you. A faithful, honorable citizen is useful to it. What position should you hold? Whatever you can hold while keeping your integrity.

Today: refuse one favor that would cost you your integrity.
meditations-7.28:
Withdraw into yourself, Marcus says. The ruling reason is content with itself when it acts justly, and that brings peace.

It's a short version of the 'inner retreat' idea from Book 4. Your mind's satisfaction doesn't depend on outcomes or approval, just on whether it has acted rightly. That's always available to return to.

Today: take a minute to step back inside yourself and ask whether you're acting justly.
meditations-7.29:
A burst of commands. Wipe out the imagination. Stop the puppet strings of impulse. Limit yourself to the present. Understand what's happening to you or to someone else. Separate each thing into its cause and its material. Think of your last hour. Leave someone's wrong where it was done.

It reads like a checklist for a turbulent moment. The last line is especially useful: don't carry other people's wrongs around with you.

Today: pick one of the seven and practice it.
meditations-7.30:
Pay attention to what is being said, Marcus says. Let your understanding get inside what's being done and who is doing it.

It's a call for real attention: not skimming conversations or events, but understanding them from the inside. Most misunderstandings and conflicts start with not quite listening.

Today: in one conversation, give your full attention to what the other person means.
meditations-7.31:
Adorn yourself with simplicity and modesty, Marcus says, and with indifference toward things that are neither virtue nor vice. Love humanity. Follow God. The poet says that law rules all, and it's enough to remember that.

'Indifference' in Stoic terms doesn't mean not caring; it means not treating money, status or comfort as good or bad in themselves. Freed from that, you can focus on loving people and acting well.

Today: choose one way to make your life a little simpler.
meditations-7.32:
About death: whether it's a scattering, a dissolving into atoms, or annihilation, it's either extinction or change.

Marcus doesn't claim to know which. He simply notes that every option is either nothing or transformation, and neither is something to dread. It's a way of facing death without needing certainty.

Today: consider one fear and ask whether any version of its outcome is truly unbearable.
meditations-7.33:
About pain: unbearable pain kills us, Marcus says, and pain that lasts is bearable. The mind keeps its own calm by withdrawing into itself, and the ruling faculty isn't made worse. As for the body parts that are hurt, let them complain if they can.

This is an old argument, from Epicurus among others: severe pain is short, and long pain is mild. Marcus, who suffered chronic illness, adds that the mind can stay intact even when the body hurts.

Today: if something hurts, notice that your judgment is still yours.
meditations-7.34:
About fame: look at the minds of those who seek it, Marcus says, and what they avoid and pursue. And just as heaps of sand pile up and bury the earlier sand, so in life later events quickly bury earlier ones.

Two points: the people whose praise you want may not have minds you admire, and whatever fame you win will soon be buried under newer news.

Today: ask whether you actually respect the people whose approval you seek.
meditations-7.35:
Marcus quotes Plato's Republic. Can a person with a lofty mind, who contemplates all time and all existence, think human life is anything great? Impossible. So such a person won't think death is an evil either.

The argument is about perspective. From a wide enough view, a single life looks small, not worthless, but not something to cling to desperately. And then death loses its terror.

Today: zoom out on one worry until it takes its proper size.
meditations-7.36:
Marcus quotes Antisthenes, a student of Socrates and a forerunner of the Cynics: 'It is royal to do good and be badly spoken of.'

For an emperor, this has extra weight. Leaders who do the right thing are often criticized for it. Antisthenes suggests that's not a sign of failure but a mark of real greatness.

Today: do one right thing even if it might draw criticism.
enchiridion-25:
Is someone preferred over you at a dinner, in being greeted or consulted? Epictetus asks. If those are good things, be glad for them. If they're bad, don't be sorry you missed them. And remember: you can't get the same rewards without paying the same price.

Lettuces cost an obol, a small coin. If someone pays and gets lettuce, and you don't pay and go without, they're not better off. They have lettuce; you have your obol. You weren't invited to dinner because you didn't pay its price: flattery and attendance. If you want it, pay. If you won't pay, don't expect it.

And you do have something instead: you didn't have to praise someone you didn't want to praise, or put up with their servants' rudeness.

Today: when you miss out on something, notice what you kept by not paying its price.
meditations-7.37:
It's shameful, Marcus says, for the face to obey the mind and compose itself as the mind commands, while the mind can't regulate and compose itself.

We're good at controlling our expressions: looking calm, pleasant or interested. Marcus says it's absurd to manage your face so well and your mind so poorly. The inner composure should come first.

Today: when you put on a calm face, check whether your mind is calm too.
meditations-7.38-43:
Marcus copied a string of lines from the Greek poets, mostly Euripides, the way people keep quotes in a notebook.

They share a theme. Don't rage at events, which don't care. Life is reaped like ripe grain: one person born, another dying. If the gods neglect me and my children, there's a reason. The good and just are on my side. And don't join in others' wailing or give way to violent emotion.

Together they sketch Stoic acceptance in poetic form: calm in the face of loss, trust in a larger order, and steadiness when others despair.

Today: pick the one line that speaks to you most and keep it with you.
meditations-7.44:
Marcus quotes Plato's Apology, Socrates' defense speech at his trial. You're wrong, Socrates says, if you think a person of any worth should calculate their chances of living or dying, rather than looking only at whether what they're doing is just or unjust, the act of a good person or a bad one.

Socrates said this while on trial for his life, and he was condemned. Marcus clearly saw him as a model of putting rightness ahead of survival.

Today: make one decision by what's right rather than by what's safe.
meditations-7.45:
More from Socrates' defense in Plato's Apology. Wherever a person has placed himself, thinking it best, or has been placed by a commander, there he should stay and face the danger, weighing nothing, not death or anything else, ahead of the shame of deserting his post.

Socrates had served as a soldier and held his ground in battle. He's saying philosophy is a post too, and he won't abandon it to save himself.

Today: stay at one post you'd be tempted to abandon when it gets uncomfortable.
meditations-7.46:
From Plato's Gorgias. Consider, my friend, whether the noble and good isn't something other than saving yourself and being saved. A real person shouldn't care about living a certain length of time or love life for its own sake. Leave that to the gods, believe the old saying that no one escapes their fate, and ask instead how to live best in the time you have.

The point is a shift in question: not 'how long?' but 'how well?'

Today: spend one hour asking how to live it well rather than how to get through it.
meditations-7.47:
Look at the courses of the stars, Marcus says, as if you were traveling with them, and keep in mind how the elements change into one another. Such thoughts wash away the grime of earthly life.

It's an invitation to the 'view from above': imagining yourself moving with the cosmos. It's meant to cleanse small preoccupations by setting them against something vast and orderly.

Today: spend a moment looking at the sky and let your worries shrink.
meditations-7.48:
A fine saying of Plato, Marcus says: whoever talks about human beings should look at earthly things as if from above. See them in their assemblies and armies, farming, marrying, making treaties, being born and dying, the noise of the law courts, empty deserts, foreign peoples, feasts, mourning, markets: a mixture of everything, and an ordered combination of opposites.

This 'view from above' is a favorite Stoic exercise. From up high, human life looks busy, varied and small, but also coherent.

Today: picture your day from a great height, as one small part of a busy world.
meditations-7.49:
Look at the past, Marcus says: the rise and fall of empires. You can foresee the future too, because it will take the same forms. It can't depart from the pattern of things now. So to have watched human life for forty years is the same as watching it for ten thousand. What more would you see?

It's a striking claim that human history repeats its shapes. Once you understand the pattern, a longer life doesn't teach much more.

Today: notice one current event that follows an old pattern.
meditations-7.50:
Marcus quotes Euripides: what grew from earth returns to earth, and what sprang from heavenly seed returns to the heavens.

He adds his own gloss: death is either the untangling of atoms or a similar scattering of the elements. Either way, things go back where they came from.

It's a calm vision of death as a return rather than a loss.

Today: think of something you'll eventually let go of as going back where it came from.
enchiridion-26:
Nature's will can be learned from things we all agree on, Epictetus says. When a neighbor's boy breaks a cup, we say, 'These things happen.' So when your cup breaks, react the same way. Now apply that to bigger things. When someone else's child or spouse dies, everyone says, 'That's part of being mortal.' But when it's our own, it's 'Alas, how wretched I am!'

We should remember how we feel when we hear the same thing about others.

It's a powerful test of consistency: the calm we offer others' losses is a guide for our own.

Today: respond to one of your own setbacks the way you'd respond to a friend's.
meditations-7.51:
Two more poetic fragments. The first mocks people who try to escape death with food, drink and magic, like diverting a river. The second, from Euripides: we must endure the wind the gods send, and work without complaint.

Together they contrast frantic avoidance with steady acceptance. No trick will keep death away; what's in our power is enduring well and working on.

Today: stop trying to avoid one unavoidable thing, and get on with your work.
meditations-7.52:
Someone else may be better at throwing an opponent in wrestling, Marcus says, but he isn't more community-minded, more modest, better prepared for whatever happens, or more patient with his neighbors' faults.

It's a reminder of which skills really matter. You may not be the best at your job, sport or talent, but you can be the best at the qualities of character that count most.

Today: let someone be better than you at something, and focus on being better at kindness.
meditations-7.53:
Wherever work can be done according to the reason shared by gods and humans, Marcus says, there's nothing to fear. Where we can benefit through successful activity that fits our nature, no harm should be suspected.

It's a reassurance about doing what's right. If you're acting in line with reason and your nature, there's no need for anxiety about whether you're doing the right thing.

Today: if you're anxious about a task, check whether it's reasonable. If it is, let the anxiety go.
meditations-7.54:
Everywhere and always, Marcus says, it's in your power to accept your present situation with reverence, to treat the people around you justly, and to work carefully on your present thoughts so nothing slips in unexamined.

Three things that are always available: accepting what is, being fair to whoever's in front of you, and checking your own thinking. No circumstance can take them away.

Today: practice all three in one ordinary moment.
meditations-7.55:
Don't look around at other people's guiding principles, Marcus says. Look straight at where nature is leading you: the universe through what happens to you, and your own nature through what you must do. Everything should act according to its makeup, and rational beings exist for one another.

He lists the first principles of human nature. First, sociability. Second, not yielding to the body's urgings, since the reasoning mind should govern the senses and appetites, not be ruled by them. Third, freedom from error and deception.

Hold to these, he says, and go straight on; then you have what is yours.

Today: test one decision against his three principles: social, self-governed, honest.
meditations-7.56:
Consider yourself already dead, Marcus says, your life complete up to now. Then live the rest, whatever is left, in harmony with nature.

It's a powerful reframing. If your life were already over, everything from here would be a bonus. That removes fear and urgency at the same time, and frees you to live the remaining time well.

Today: treat the rest of today as extra time, and use it well.
meditations-7.57:
Love only what happens to you and is spun into your destiny, Marcus says. What could suit you better?

It's a step beyond acceptance. Nietzsche later called this attitude amor fati, love of fate. Marcus suggests that what actually happens to you is, by definition, what fits your life, so why not embrace it?

Today: find something to appreciate in one thing you'd rather hadn't happened.
meditations-7.58:
Whenever something happens, Marcus says, picture others it happened to, who were upset, found it strange and complained. Where are they now? Nowhere. Why copy them?

Leave those reactions to people who cause them and people swayed by them. Focus entirely on how to make good use of what happens. Then you'll use it well, and it will become material for you to work on. Just attend to yourself and resolve to be good in every act. The passage then breaks off in the original.

Today: when something goes wrong, skip the complaining and ask how to use it.
meditations-7.59:
Look within, Marcus says. Within is the fountain of good, and it will always bubble up if you keep digging.

The image is of a spring that never runs dry, but needs effort to keep flowing. Goodness isn't something you get from outside; it's in you already, and the work is in keeping it clear.

Today: dig a little: do one good thing that requires effort.
meditations-7.60:
The body should be steady, Marcus says, without awkwardness in movement or posture. Just as the mind shows intelligence and decency in the face, so the whole body should. But all without affectation.

It's a reminder that character shows physically. How you stand, walk and move can express calm and self-possession, but it shouldn't be a performance.

Today: notice your posture and movement, and let them reflect a calm mind.
enchiridion-27:
A target isn't set up to be missed, Epictetus says, and in the same way the nature of evil doesn't exist in the world.

The idea, explained in the translator's note, is that happiness, the result of virtue, is the target set for us. Missing it isn't something built into the world; it's our own failure to aim well. Evil isn't a positive force but a miss.

Today: when things go wrong, ask how you might aim better, rather than blaming the world.
meditations-7.61:
The art of living is more like wrestling than dancing, Marcus says, in that it must stand ready and firm to meet sudden, unexpected attacks.

A dancer follows choreography. A wrestler has to respond to whatever the opponent does. Life doesn't follow a script, so the skill isn't grace in a planned routine but readiness for surprises.

Today: when something unexpected happens, respond like a wrestler, steady and ready.
meditations-7.62:
Keep looking at whose approval you want, Marcus says, and what guiding principles they have. Then you won't blame people who offend without meaning to, and you won't want their approval, once you see where their opinions and desires come from.

Examining the people we want to impress usually lowers their hold on us. Their judgments come from their own limitations, which also makes it easier to forgive them.

Today: think of someone whose approval you crave, and look honestly at their values.
meditations-7.63:
Every soul, the philosopher says, is unwillingly deprived of truth, Marcus writes, and in the same way of justice, self-control, kindness and the rest. Keep this in mind constantly, and you'll be gentler with everyone.

The idea comes from Plato via Epictetus: no one chooses to be wrong. People who behave badly don't want to be mistaken; they genuinely misjudge what's good. Seeing that softens anger into patience.

Today: assume one person who annoys you is mistaken, not wicked.
meditations-7.64:
In any pain, Marcus says, remember there's no disgrace in it, and it doesn't make your mind worse, either as rational or as social. For most pains, he borrows Epicurus: pain is neither unbearable nor endless, if you remember its limits and add nothing to it in imagination.

He adds a sharp observation: many discomforts we don't call pain, like sleepiness, heat or loss of appetite, are really the same thing. When they annoy you, recognize you're giving in to pain.

Today: notice one minor discomfort and refuse to add a story to it.
meditations-7.65:
Be careful, Marcus says, not to feel toward the inhuman the way they feel toward humans.

It's a warning against becoming what you oppose. When people treat others cruelly, it's tempting to answer with the same coldness. But then you've let them shape your character.

Today: respond to unkindness without becoming unkind.
meditations-7.66:
How do we know, Marcus asks, that Telauges, a son of Pythagoras, wasn't better than Socrates? It isn't enough that Socrates died more nobly, argued more skilfully, endured cold nights better, or refused the Thirty Tyrants' order to arrest Leon of Salamis. We should ask what kind of soul he had.

Was he content with being just to people and reverent to the gods? Not pointlessly upset by others' wickedness, not enslaved to anyone's ignorance, not surprised or crushed by his lot, not letting his mind be swayed by the body's feelings?

The lesson: judge people by their inner character, not their famous deeds.

Today: judge someone by their character rather than their achievements.
meditations-7.67:
Nature hasn't fused your mind so tightly to your body, Marcus says, that you can't draw a boundary around yourself and take charge of what's yours. It's entirely possible to be a godlike person and be recognized by no one.

And very little is needed to live happily. Just because you've given up hope of becoming a great logician or scientist, don't give up hope of being free, modest, community-minded and obedient to God.

It's encouraging: you don't need special talents to be good.

Today: let go of one ambition you won't reach, and focus on one quality you can.
meditations-7.68:
You can live free of all compulsion, Marcus says, in perfect peace of mind, even if the whole world shouts against you and wild beasts tear your body apart. What stops the mind from staying calm and judging things justly?

Your judgment can say to each thing: 'This is what you really are, whatever people think.' And your use of it can say: 'You're just what I was looking for.' Whatever happens is always material for virtue and skill.

Nothing that happens is new or unmanageable. It's ordinary, workable material.

Today: greet one difficulty with 'you're exactly what I needed to practice on.'
meditations-7.69:
The perfection of character, Marcus says, is to live each day as if it were your last: neither frantic, nor sluggish, nor pretending.

The 'last day' idea isn't about panic or indulgence. It's about living with the right intensity: fully engaged without frenzy, calm without apathy, and sincere throughout.

Today: live today with steady attention, as if it mattered completely.
enchiridion-28:
If someone handed your body over to any passer-by, Epictetus says, you'd be furious. Aren't you ashamed to hand over your mind to anyone who insults you, letting them upset and confuse you?

It's a vivid comparison. We'd never let a stranger control our body, yet we routinely let them control our mood with a few words.

Today: when someone tries to provoke you, keep your mind your own.
meditations-7.70:
The immortal gods aren't upset, Marcus says, at having to tolerate so many bad people for so long; they even take care of them in every way. And you, who'll be gone so soon, are tired of putting up with bad people, when you're one of them yourself?

The last twist is pointed. We tire of others' faults while forgetting our own. If the gods can be patient forever, we can manage a few decades.

Today: be patient with one person whose faults you share.
meditations-7.71:
It's ridiculous, Marcus says, not to flee your own wickedness, which you can do, but to try to flee other people's, which you can't.

We often put our energy into avoiding or changing others, which is outside our control, while neglecting our own faults, which are entirely within it.

Today: work on one fault of your own instead of complaining about someone else's.
