meditations-7.72:
Whatever the rational and social faculty finds to be neither intelligent nor social, Marcus says, it rightly judges inferior to itself.

It's a standard for evaluating things: does this involve reason, and does it serve others? If not, it ranks below the mind that's judging it. That keeps you from being impressed or controlled by things that lack either.

Today: test one thing that grips you: is it reasonable, and is it social?
meditations-7.73:
When you've done a good deed and someone has benefited, Marcus asks, why look for a third thing, as fools do: credit for having done it, or something in return?

The good act and the benefit are complete in themselves. Wanting recognition or repayment adds nothing to the good and turns generosity into a transaction.

Today: help someone and let the act be the whole of it.
meditations-7.74:
No one gets tired of receiving what's useful, Marcus says. And acting according to nature is useful. So don't get tired of receiving that benefit by giving it to others.

The argument is neat: doing good is itself good for you. Helping others isn't a drain; it's a way of benefiting yourself through your own nature.

Today: when helping feels tiring, remember you're also receiving something.
meditations-7.75:
The nature of the whole set out to make the universe, Marcus says. So either everything that happens follows from that, or even the most important things the universe aims at are governed by no reason at all. Remembering this will make you calmer about many things.

It's a compact version of his usual either-or. If there's order, what happens is part of it. If there isn't, there's nothing to resent. Either way, agitation doesn't help.

Today: when something seems unfair, ask whether resenting it helps under either view.
meditations-8.1:
Another cure for wanting empty fame, Marcus says: you can no longer claim to have lived your whole life, or even your adult life, as a philosopher. Others can see it, and so can you. Your life has been too messy, and your position as emperor stands in the way.

So drop the question of how you'll look, and be content to live the rest of your life as your nature wants. You've wandered a lot and found happiness nowhere: not in clever arguments, wealth, reputation or pleasure.

Where is it, then? In doing what human nature requires, guided by the belief that nothing is good unless it makes you just, self-controlled, brave and free.

Today: let go of how you seem, and do one thing that makes you better.
meditations-8.2:
Before every action, Marcus says, ask: how does this affect me? Will I regret it? In a little while I'll be dead and everything gone. If what I'm doing now is the work of a thinking, social being under the same law as God, what more do I need?

It's a quick ethical check: would I regret this, and is it worthy of what I am? Mortality makes the question clearer, not more anxious.

Today: before one decision, ask whether you'll regret it.
meditations-8.3:
Alexander, Julius Caesar and Pompey, Marcus asks: what are they compared with Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates? The philosophers understood things, their causes and their substance, and their minds were their own. The conquerors had so many things to manage, and were slaves to so many.

It's a striking reversal from an emperor. The men with the most power were the least free; the men with almost nothing were masters of themselves.

Today: notice one thing you think you control that actually controls you.
enchiridion-29:
In every undertaking, Epictetus says, consider what comes before and after, and only then begin. Otherwise you'll start enthusiastically and quit in shame.

'I want to win at the Olympics.' Then consider the discipline, diet, training in heat and cold, the injuries, the dust, and the chance of losing anyway. If you still want it, go ahead. Otherwise you'll be like children who play at wrestling one day and tragedy the next, an ape copying whatever impresses you, serious about nothing.

The same goes for philosophy. You'll have to work, watch yourself, give up some appetites and friends, be laughed at, and come off worse in honors and offices. If you want calm and freedom at that price, come. If not, don't flit between roles. Be one person: cultivate your reason or chase externals.

Today: before starting something new, honestly count its costs.
meditations-8.4:
People will keep doing the same things, Marcus says, even if you burst with frustration.

It's a dry, almost funny line. Getting worked up won't change other people's habits. You can influence, persuade or set an example, but exploding over it only hurts you.

Today: notice one thing you're straining against that won't change, and stop straining.
meditations-8.5:
This is the main thing, Marcus says: don't be disturbed, because everything follows the nature of the whole, and soon you'll be nobody and nowhere, like Hadrian and Augustus.

Next, look steadily at the task in front of you, remember your duty is to be a good person, and do what human nature asks without swerving. Speak as seems most just to you, but kindly, modestly and without pretense.

The passage moves from perspective to action: stay calm, then get on with being good.

Today: focus on your next task and do it as a good person would.
meditations-8.6:
Nature's work, Marcus says, is to move things from here to there, to change them, take them away and carry them elsewhere. Everything is change, but there's nothing new to fear. Everything is familiar; only the arrangement shifts.

It's a reassuring way to see change: not as strange or threatening, but as the same old materials being rearranged.

Today: see one change as a rearrangement rather than a loss.
meditations-8.7:
Every nature is content when it's going well, Marcus says. A rational nature goes well when it agrees to nothing false or uncertain, aims its actions only at the common good, limits its desires and aversions to what's in its power, and accepts what the common nature gives it.

Your nature is part of that larger nature, as a leaf's nature is part of a plant's. But unlike a leaf, you belong to a nature that can't be obstructed, and that is intelligent and just, giving everything its fair share.

The four tests are a practical summary of Stoic living: clear thinking, social action, desires within your control, and acceptance.

Today: check yourself against one of the four tests.
meditations-8.8:
You don't have time to read, Marcus tells himself. But you do have time to check your arrogance. Time to rise above pleasure and pain. Time to rise above love of fame. Time not to be irritated by foolish, ungrateful people, and even to care for them.

Busy as an emperor at war, he couldn't study as he wanted. His answer: the practice of philosophy doesn't need books or leisure. It happens in how you handle each moment.

Today: practice one virtue in a moment you'd usually call too busy.
meditations-8.9:
Let no one hear you complaining any more about court life, Marcus says, or about your own.

It's a blunt resolution. Complaining changes nothing and spreads discontent. For an emperor stuck in palace politics, it was a promise to himself to stop grumbling about his situation and deal with it.

Today: go one day without complaining about your work or your life.
meditations-8.10:
Regret, Marcus says, is a kind of self-reproach for having neglected something useful. What's good must be useful, and a good person would care about it. But no good person ever regretted turning down a sensual pleasure. So pleasure is neither good nor useful.

It's a clever argument. Nobody looks back and says, 'I wish I'd indulged more.' That suggests pleasure isn't the kind of thing that matters most.

Today: think of a pleasure you passed up, and notice that you don't regret it.
meditations-8.11:
Marcus gives himself a set of questions to apply to anything. What is this in itself? What's it made of? What's its cause or form? What's it doing in the world? How long will it last?

It's a tool for cutting through impressions. Many things that seem impressive or frightening look smaller once you analyze what they actually are and how long they'll be around.

Today: run those five questions on one thing that's bothering you.
meditations-8.12:
When you're reluctant to get out of bed, Marcus says, remember that it's your nature, human nature, to do things for others, while sleep is something even animals do. What fits your own nature is more truly yours, more suitable and even more enjoyable.

It's a gentler version of his famous 'getting up' passage. Rising to do something worthwhile is more yours than staying in bed. It's also, he suggests, more satisfying.

Today: when you're reluctant to start, remind yourself what you're getting up for.
meditations-8.13:
Constantly, Marcus says, and if possible with every impression, apply the principles of physics, ethics and logic.

These were the three branches of Stoic philosophy. Physics: understand what the thing really is and how it fits into nature. Ethics: ask whether it's truly good or bad. Logic: check whether your reasoning about it holds up.

It's a full toolkit for thinking clearly about anything.

Today: apply all three to one thing that grabs your attention.
enchiridion-30:
Duties are measured by relationships, Epictetus says. Is someone your father? Then you owe him care, deference and patience with his criticism. 'But he's a bad father.' Were you naturally bound to a good father? No, just to a father. Is your brother unfair? Keep your own side of the relationship fair. Don't look at what he does, but at what you must do to keep your will in line with nature. No one can hurt you unless you allow it.

Apply this to every role: neighbor, citizen, commander. Each relationship tells you your duties, regardless of how the other person behaves.

Today: fulfill your part in one relationship, whatever the other person is doing.
meditations-8.14:
Whenever you meet someone, Marcus says, ask yourself right away: what are this person's beliefs about good and bad? If you know what they think about pleasure and pain, fame and disgrace, life and death, nothing they do will surprise you. And remember they're in a sense compelled to act that way.

It's a powerful tool for understanding people. Behavior follows from beliefs. Once you see someone's values, their actions make sense, even when they're wrong.

Today: with one person who puzzles you, try to identify what they believe is good.
meditations-8.15:
It's shameful to be surprised that a fig tree produces figs, Marcus says, and equally shameful to be surprised that the world produces the things it produces. A doctor shouldn't be shocked by a fever, nor a helmsman by a headwind.

We often act surprised by things that are entirely predictable: rudeness, setbacks, illness. Professionals expect the problems of their field. We should expect the problems of life.

Today: when something goes wrong, ask whether it was really that surprising.
meditations-8.16:
Changing your mind and following someone who corrects you, Marcus says, is just as free as sticking to your mistake. The act is still yours, carried out by your own judgment and understanding.

This addresses a common fear: that admitting you're wrong is a kind of defeat. Marcus says no. Choosing to accept a better view is your own free act, not a surrender.

Today: change your mind about one thing when you're shown a better reason.
meditations-8.17:
If something is in your power, why do it wrong? Marcus asks. If it's in someone else's power, who are you blaming: chance or the gods? Both are foolish. Blame no one.

If you can, fix the cause. If not, fix the thing itself. If you can't even do that, what's the point of complaining? Nothing should be done without a purpose.

It's a practical flowchart for frustration: fix what you can, accept what you can't, and drop blame entirely.

Today: when you're about to blame someone, ask what you can fix instead.
meditations-8.18:
What dies doesn't fall out of the universe, Marcus says. It stays here, changes here, and breaks down into its parts, which are the elements of the universe and of you. Those change too, and they don't complain.

It's a calming image of death as continuity. Nothing is truly lost; it's recycled into the same world we live in. And the elements accept their change without protest.

Today: think of one loss as part of an ongoing change rather than a disappearance.
meditations-8.19:
Everything exists for a purpose, Marcus says: a horse, a vine. Why be surprised? Even the sun would say, 'I exist for some purpose,' and so would the other gods. So what are you for? Pleasure? See if common sense allows that.

The question is direct: if everything has a function, what's yours? Marcus's answer, throughout the book, is to be rational and social, to think well and to serve others.

Today: ask yourself what you're for, and do one thing that answers it.
meditations-8.20:
Nature cares as much about the end of things as about their beginning and middle, Marcus says, like someone throwing a ball. What good is it to the ball to go up, or harm to come down, or even to have landed? What good is it to a bubble to hold together, or harm to burst? The same goes for a lamp.

The images are light, almost playful. A ball, a bubble and a flame each have a full arc, and the end is part of the design, not a failure.

Today: see one ending as the natural completion of an arc.
meditations-8.21:
Turn the body inside out, Marcus says, and see what it's like, and what it becomes when it's old or diseased.

Then: the one who praises and the one who is praised, the one who remembers and the one who is remembered, are all short-lived, in a small corner of the world. Not even there does everyone agree, nor does anyone agree with himself. And the whole earth is a point.

It's a deliberately unglamorous view of the body and of fame, meant to loosen vanity's grip.

Today: when you're tempted to worry about your image, remember how small and brief it is.
meditations-8.22:
Pay attention to whatever's in front of you, Marcus says, whether it's a thought, an action or a word.

Then he turns on himself: you deserve what you're suffering, because you'd rather become good tomorrow than be good today.

The second line is one of his sharpest. Procrastinating on character is still procrastinating, and it has consequences.

Today: do the good thing today rather than planning to tomorrow.
enchiridion-31:
True piety, Epictetus says, is holding right beliefs about the gods: that they exist and govern the world justly and well, and resolving to follow them willingly in everything. Then you'll never blame them or feel neglected.

But that's only possible if you place good and bad only in what's in your power. Otherwise, when you don't get what you want, you'll blame whoever you think caused it. That's why sons curse fathers who withhold what seems good, and why the brothers Polynices and Eteocles killed each other over a throne. Farmers, sailors and the bereaved curse the gods for the same reason.

So managing your desires is also how you keep your reverence. And offer the customary rites sincerely, neither stingily nor extravagantly.

Today: notice one resentment that comes from wanting something outside your control.
meditations-8.23:
Am I doing something? Marcus asks. I do it for the good of humanity. Does something happen to me? I accept it and refer it to the gods, the source from which everything comes.

It's a two-part rule for living. Your actions point outward to others. What happens to you, you receive as part of the order of things. Both keep you from self-absorption.

Today: link one action to the good of others, and accept one event without complaint.
meditations-8.24:
Just as bathing looks to you, oil, sweat, dirt, grimy water, all disgusting, Marcus says, so is every part of life and everything in it.

Roman bathing involved scraping oil and grime off the skin. Marcus uses that unglamorous image to strip the glamour from life generally. It isn't contempt but a check on overvaluing things.

Today: look at one thing you prize in plain, unflattering terms.
meditations-8.25:
A litany of the dead. Lucilla, Marcus's mother, saw her husband Verus die, then died herself. Secunda saw Maximus die, then died. Antoninus saw his wife Faustina die, then died. Celer saw Hadrian die, then died. And the clever men, the seers and the proud, Charax, Demetrius, Eudaemon: all gone. Some weren't remembered even briefly, some became legends, others vanished even from legends.

So remember: this little compound, you, will either be dissolved, or your breath will go out, or move somewhere else.

The repetition is the point. Each mourner becomes the mourned.

Today: think of someone you've lost, and be gentle with someone who's still here.
meditations-8.26:
It's satisfying for a person to do the work proper to a person, Marcus says. And that work is to be kind to your own kind, to look down on the pull of the senses, to judge plausible appearances correctly, and to study the nature of the universe and what happens in it.

He lists four human tasks: kindness, self-mastery, clear judgment and understanding. Doing them is not a burden but the source of real satisfaction.

Today: practice one of the four, and notice the satisfaction it brings.
meditations-8.27:
You have three relationships, Marcus says: to the body that surrounds you, to the divine cause from which everything comes, and to the people you live with.

It's a simple map of a life. Each relationship asks something different: care for the body without being ruled by it, acceptance of the larger order, and fairness and kindness toward others.

Today: give a little attention to each of the three.
meditations-8.28:
Pain is either bad for the body, Marcus says, in which case let the body say what it thinks, or bad for the soul. But the soul can keep its own calm and not judge pain to be evil. Every judgment, impulse, desire and aversion is inside, and no evil can climb that high.

The body feels pain; the mind decides what it means. Marcus suffered from chronic illness, so this wasn't theoretical for him.

Today: if you feel pain or discomfort, notice it without calling it a disaster.
meditations-8.29:
Wipe out your imaginings, Marcus says, by often telling yourself: it's in my power right now to keep this soul free of badness, desire and agitation. I look at things, see what they are, and use each according to its worth. Remember this power you have by nature.

It's a self-reminder you can actually repeat. Agitation often comes from runaway thoughts; naming your power to stop them is a way of using it.

Today: when your mind races, say his sentence to yourself.
meditations-8.30:
Speak in the senate and to every person, whoever they are, appropriately, Marcus says, without affectation. Use plain speech.

From an emperor, it's a commitment to talk the same way to the powerful and to anyone else: clearly, honestly and without putting on airs.

Today: say one thing plainly that you'd usually dress up.
meditations-8.31:
Augustus's court, Marcus says: his wife, daughter, descendants, ancestors, sister, his general Agrippa, relatives, friends, the philosopher Areius, his adviser Maecenas, doctors and priests. The whole court is dead.

Then think of whole families, like the Pompeii, and the tombstones reading 'The last of his line.' Think of how hard their ancestors worked to leave heirs, and that someone has to be last. Consider the death of an entire family.

It's a meditation on how even dynasties end.

Today: let go of one effort to secure your legacy, and invest in the present instead.
enchiridion-32:
When you consult a fortune-teller, Epictetus says, remember you don't know what will happen, but you already know what kind of thing it will be, if you're a philosopher. If it's outside your control, it's neither good nor bad. So don't go trembling with desire or dread. Know that whatever happens, you can make good use of it.

Consult oracles only, as Socrates advised, when reason can't settle the question. But when your duty is to share a friend's or your country's danger, don't ask the oracle whether to do it. Even if the signs predict death, exile or injury, reason tells you to stand by them.

Listen to the greater oracle, Apollo, who once threw out of his temple a man who had failed to save his friend.

Today: when facing a duty, don't wait for a guarantee of a good outcome.
meditations-8.32:
Your job is to order your life well act by act, Marcus says. If each act does its part as far as possible, be content. No one can stop that.

'But something outside will get in the way.' Nothing can stop you acting justly, soberly and thoughtfully. 'But some other action might be blocked.' Then accept the obstacle, shift your effort to what's possible, and another opportunity will appear in its place.

It's practical resilience: when one path closes, the next right action is still available.

Today: when something blocks you, look for the next good action that's still open.
meditations-8.33:
Accept wealth or good fortune without arrogance, Marcus says, and be ready to let it go.

It's a brief and balanced attitude toward success. Stoics don't reject good things, but they hold them loosely. Enjoy them without pride, and lose them without despair.

Today: enjoy one good thing in your life while remembering it isn't permanent.
meditations-8.34:
If you've ever seen a severed hand, foot or head lying apart from the body, Marcus says, that's what a person makes of himself when he resents what happens, cuts himself off from others or acts antisocially.

But there's a beautiful provision: you can reattach yourself. No other part, once cut off, can rejoin the whole. Yet God gave humans that kindness: not only to stay connected, but to return and resume their place.

It's a hopeful passage. Alienation is never final; you can always rejoin.

Today: reconnect with one person or group you've drifted from.
meditations-8.35:
Nature has given every rational being its powers, Marcus says, including this one. Just as the universe takes whatever opposes it and fits it into its plan, a rational being can turn every obstacle into material for its own purposes.

It's another version of his recurring theme: obstacles aren't just in the way, they can be used. That ability isn't luck; it's part of what you are.

Today: take one obstacle and use it as material for something.
meditations-8.36:
Don't upset yourself by picturing your whole life at once, Marcus says. Don't let your mind gather up every trouble you might face. Instead, in each moment, ask: what about this is unbearable? You'll be embarrassed to answer.

Remember, it's not the future or the past that hurts you, only the present. And the present shrinks to very little if you isolate it, and scold your mind if it can't hold out even against that.

It's a classic technique: take difficulty one moment at a time.

Today: when overwhelmed, ask what's actually unbearable right now.
meditations-8.37:
Do the companions of dead emperors still sit by their tombs? Marcus asks. That would be absurd. And if they did, would the dead know? Would they be pleased? Would it make them immortal? Weren't those mourners destined to grow old and die too? And then what?

His conclusion is blunt: 'all this is stink and blood in a bag.' He means the body and its attachments are temporary.

It's a harsh passage, but it targets the hope that devotion or memory can defeat death.

Today: love the living while they're here, rather than worrying about how you'll be mourned.
meditations-8.38:
'If you can see clearly, look and judge wisely,' says the philosopher.

Marcus quotes an unnamed thinker. The advice is simple: if you have the capacity to see things as they are, use it, and let it guide your judgment. Clear sight is wasted if you still judge carelessly.

Today: look at one situation carefully before deciding what you think.
meditations-8.39:
In the makeup of a rational being, Marcus says, I see no virtue opposed to justice. But I do see a virtue opposed to love of pleasure: self-control.

The observation is subtle. Nothing in our nature works against justice. But we do have an inner check on pleasure-seeking. That suggests justice is central to who we are, and pleasure is something to be governed.

Today: practice self-control with one pleasure.
meditations-8.40:
If you take away your opinion about what seems to hurt you, Marcus says, you yourself are completely safe. 'Who is this self?' Your reason. 'But I'm not just reason.' Fine. Then let reason not disturb itself, and if some other part of you suffers, let it have its own opinion.

It's a small dialogue about identity. The Stoics locate the true self in the reasoning mind. Even if other parts hurt, that part can stay calm.

Today: when part of you feels bad, let the reasoning part of you stay steady.
meditations-8.41:
Obstacles to the senses are bad for an animal, Marcus says. Obstacles to its impulses are too. So obstacles to the intellect are bad for a rational being.

Apply this to yourself. Pain or pleasure? Let the senses deal with it. Something blocking your efforts? If you were pursuing it without reservation, that's a real obstacle. But if you allowed for how things usually go, you haven't been harmed or even blocked.

And the things proper to the mind can't be obstructed by fire, iron, tyrant or insult. Once it has become a perfect sphere, it stays a sphere.

Today: pursue one goal with a reservation, 'if nothing prevents it.'
enchiridion-33:
Epictetus gives a set of rules for daily conduct. Decide on a character for yourself and keep it, alone and in company.

Be mostly silent, or say only what's needed, briefly. Avoid small talk about sport, food and especially gossip about people. If you can, steer conversation toward better topics; among strangers, keep quiet. Don't laugh loudly or constantly. Avoid oaths. Be careful at vulgar entertainments, since bad company rubs off.

Take only what the body needs; cut out show and luxury. Don't be self-righteous about others' choices.

If you're told someone speaks ill of you, don't defend yourself; say, 'He didn't know my other faults, or he'd have mentioned those too.' At public shows, want only what happens, and don't rave about it afterward.

Before meeting someone important, think how Socrates or Zeno would act. Expect to be kept waiting or ignored, and if it's your duty to go, go anyway without complaining. Don't keep telling stories about yourself, don't play for laughs, and show displeasure at crude talk.

Today: pick one rule from his list and follow it all day.
meditations-8.42:
It isn't right that I should cause myself pain, Marcus says, since I've never deliberately caused pain to anyone else.

It's a gentle argument for self-compassion. If you'd never hurt others on purpose, why would you torment yourself with harsh thoughts and needless worry? Treat yourself with the same consideration you show others.

Today: notice one way you're being harder on yourself than you'd ever be on someone else.
meditations-8.43:
Different things delight different people, Marcus says. My delight is keeping my mind sound: not turning away from any person or anything that happens, but looking at everything with welcoming eyes and using each thing according to its worth.

It's an appealing picture of contentment: a mind open to whatever comes, neither rejecting people nor events, and able to make good use of them.

Today: greet one unwelcome person or event with open eyes.
meditations-8.44:
Make sure you hold on to the present, Marcus says. People who chase fame after death forget that future generations will be just like the people they can't stand now, and just as mortal. What is it to you if they make some sound or hold some opinion about you?

The argument deflates posthumous fame. If you don't value your contemporaries' opinions, why value those of people who will be no different?

Today: invest in the present instead of in how you'll be remembered.
meditations-8.45:
Take me and throw me where you like, Marcus says. There I'll keep my inner self calm and content, as long as it can feel and act according to its nature. Is a change of place reason for my soul to be miserable, worse than before, depressed, overexcited, cringing or afraid? What could ever be reason enough?

It's a declaration of portable peace. Your circumstances can change completely, but your inner state is yours to keep.

Today: if your situation changes unexpectedly, keep your inner state steady.
meditations-8.46:
Nothing can happen to a person that isn't a human event, Marcus says, nor to an ox that isn't natural to oxen, nor to a vine that isn't natural to vines, nor to a stone that isn't proper to stones. If everything gets what is usual and natural for it, why complain? Nature brings nothing you can't bear.

It's a reminder that human troubles are human-sized. What happens to us is the kind of thing that happens to people, and people are built to endure it.

Today: remind yourself that whatever you face is a human-sized problem.
meditations-8.47:
If something outside you causes you pain, Marcus says, it's not the thing that disturbs you but your judgment of it, and you can wipe that judgment out right now. If something in your own character pains you, who stops you correcting your view? And if you're upset at not doing something you think right, why not act instead of complaining?

'But there's an obstacle I can't overcome.' Then don't grieve; it's not your fault. 'But life isn't worth living if I can't do it.' Then leave life calmly, as someone who dies while fully active, at peace even with the obstacles.

Today: when you complain about something, ask whether you could act on it instead.
meditations-8.48:
Remember, Marcus says, that the ruling faculty is unconquerable when it gathers itself and is content, doing nothing it doesn't choose to do, even if it resists out of sheer stubbornness. How much stronger, then, when it judges carefully with the help of reason?

That's why a mind free of passions is a citadel. A person has no safer fortress to retreat to and be impregnable from then on. Not seeing this is ignorance; seeing it and not taking refuge there is misery.

The 'inner citadel' is one of the book's best-known images: a mind that can't be stormed from outside.

Today: when pressure builds, retreat into your own judgment and hold it.
meditations-8.49:
Don't tell yourself more than first impressions report, Marcus says. Someone tells you a person is speaking badly of you. That's what was reported; that you've been harmed was not. I see my child is ill. I see that; that he's in danger, I don't see.

So stick with first impressions and add nothing from inside, and nothing will happen to you. Or if you add anything, add it as someone who understands how the world works.

It's one of the most practical Stoic tools: separate the bare facts from the stories you attach to them.

Today: when you hear bad news, state only the facts, without the story.
meditations-8.50:
The cucumber's bitter? Throw it away. There are brambles on the path? Step around them. That's enough. Don't add, 'Why are such things in the world?' Marcus says. Someone who understands nature would laugh at you, as a carpenter or shoemaker would laugh if you complained about shavings and scraps in their workshop.

And nature is even cleverer than they are. Craftsmen have somewhere to throw their scraps; nature has no outside. Yet everything that seems to decay or become useless, she turns back into herself and makes new things from it.

It's a favorite passage for its practicality: deal with the problem, skip the cosmic complaint.

Today: handle one annoyance without asking why it exists.
enchiridion-34:
When some promised pleasure dazzles you, Epictetus says, don't get swept away. Put it off and give yourself time. Then picture two moments: enjoying the pleasure, and regretting it afterward. Set against those how pleased you'll be with yourself if you resist.

And even if it seems the right time to indulge, don't let its charm overpower you. Remember how much better it feels to know you've won such a victory.

It's a practical technique: delay, then imagine the aftermath, then imagine the satisfaction of restraint.

Today: delay one temptation and picture how you'll feel afterward either way.
meditations-8.51:
Don't be sluggish in action, Marcus says, muddled in conversation or scattered in thought. Don't let your soul be torn within or spill over without. And don't be so busy you have no leisure.

Suppose people kill you, cut you up, curse you. How does that stop your mind being pure, wise, sober and just? Someone standing at a clear spring and cursing it can't stop it giving fresh water. If he throws in mud or filth, it soon washes them out and stays clean.

How do you become a living spring rather than a stagnant well? By training yourself every hour in freedom, together with contentment, simplicity and modesty.

Today: let one insult wash through you like mud through a spring.
meditations-8.52:
Whoever doesn't know what the world is, Marcus says, doesn't know where he is. Whoever doesn't know what the world is for doesn't know who he is, or what the world is. And whoever fails in either couldn't even say what he himself is for.

So what do you think of someone who chases, or fears, the applause of people who don't know where they are or who they are?

It's a sharp way of deflating the crowd's approval. If the audience doesn't understand the basics of life, their applause tells you little.

Today: ask whether the people you want to impress really understand what matters.
meditations-8.53:
Do you want praise from someone who curses himself three times an hour? Marcus asks. Do you want to please someone who doesn't please himself? Does someone please himself who regrets nearly everything he does?

The questions expose how odd it is to seek approval from people who are at war with themselves. Their judgment can't be steady if their own lives aren't.

Today: notice whose approval you're seeking, and whether they're at peace with themselves.
meditations-8.54:
Don't just let your breathing harmonize with the surrounding air, Marcus says. Let your mind harmonize with the mind that embraces all things. Reason is spread through everything and available to anyone who wants to draw it in, just as air is available to anyone who can breathe.

The breathing analogy is lovely. Reason isn't scarce; it's all around you, like air. You just have to take it in.

Today: pause and take a few slow breaths, and let your thinking settle as your breathing does.
meditations-8.55:
In general, wickedness does no harm to the universe, Marcus says. And one person's wickedness doesn't harm anyone else. It only harms the one who has it, and he can be free of it whenever he chooses.

The Stoic claim is that vice injures only its owner. Others may suffer losses, but their character, their real self, is untouched unless they let it be. And the vicious person can always change.

Today: remember that someone else's bad behavior can't make you worse unless you let it.
meditations-8.56:
To my will, Marcus says, my neighbor's will is as indifferent as his breath and flesh. We're made for one another, but each of us has a mind with its own job. Otherwise my neighbor's wickedness would be my harm, and God didn't intend my unhappiness to depend on someone else.

It's a careful balance. We're bound together, but each person's character is their own responsibility. No one else can make you bad, which also means no one else holds your happiness hostage.

Today: let one person's choice be theirs, without making it your burden.
meditations-8.57:
Sunlight seems to pour down in every direction, Marcus says, but it isn't poured out and lost; it stretches out. That's why the Greek word for its rays comes from 'to extend'. Watch light come through a narrow opening into a dark room: it travels in a straight line, and when it hits a solid object it stops there and lights it up, without sliding off or falling away.

The mind should spread like that: extending rather than spilling, meeting obstacles without violent collision, staying fixed and lighting up whatever receives it. Anything that refuses the light simply goes without it.

Today: when you meet resistance, stay steady and keep shedding light rather than forcing your way.
meditations-8.58:
Whoever fears death, Marcus says, fears either losing sensation or having a different kind. If there's no sensation, you'll feel no harm. If there's a different kind, you'll be a different kind of living being, and you won't have stopped living.

It's a classic argument that death, considered calmly, offers nothing to fear: either nothing at all, or a continuation in another form.

Today: when fear of an ending comes up, work through what you're actually afraid of.
meditations-8.59:
'People exist for one another. So teach them, or bear with them.'

That's Marcus's whole approach to difficult people in two sentences. Since we're made to live together, there are only two good responses to someone's faults: help them improve, or patiently put up with them. Anger and contempt aren't on the list.

Today: with one difficult person, choose to teach or to bear with them.
enchiridion-35:
When you do something because you've clearly judged it should be done, Epictetus says, don't avoid being seen doing it, even if most people will misunderstand. If you're not acting rightly, avoid the act itself. If you are, why fear those who criticize you wrongly?

It's a call for courage in your convictions. Hiding a right action suggests you don't trust it. Either it's wrong, so don't do it, or it's right, so do it openly.

Today: do one right thing openly, even if it might be misunderstood.
meditations-8.60:
An arrow moves one way, Marcus says, the mind another. But the mind, whether it's being cautious or investigating, still moves straight on toward its goal.

The comparison is subtle. An arrow flies directly. The mind may pause, circle, weigh options or hold back, but if it's working well, all of that is still progress toward its aim.

Today: when you're hesitating carefully over something, remember that careful thought still counts as moving forward.
meditations-8.61:
Enter into every person's mind, Marcus says, and let every person enter into yours.

It's an ideal of mutual understanding and openness. Try to understand how others think, and be transparent enough that they can understand you. It's the opposite of guardedness and suspicion.

Today: try to understand one person's view fully, and share your own honestly.
meditations-9.1:
Marcus argues that injustice is impiety, an offense against the divine. Nature made rational beings to help one another, never to harm each other, so injustice breaks her will. Lying is impious too, since nature is also truth. Even unintentional lying sets you against nature, because you've neglected the faculty that tells true from false.

Pursuing pleasure as good and fleeing pain as evil is impious as well. It makes you accuse nature of unfairness, since bad people often enjoy pleasure and good people suffer pain. It makes you fear what will happen, and pleasure-seekers won't hold back from injustice.

Nature treats pleasure and pain, life and death, honor and dishonor evenly. To follow nature, so should you.

Today: treat one pleasure and one discomfort with the same calm.
meditations-9.2:
The happiest thing, Marcus says, would be to leave the world without ever tasting lying, hypocrisy, luxury and pride. The next best is to leave once you're fed up with them.

Have you decided to stay with vice? Hasn't experience taught you to flee this plague? Corruption of the mind is a far worse plague than any pestilence in the air. That one harms us as animals; this one harms us as human beings.

Writing during the Antonine Plague, which devastated the empire, Marcus pointedly calls moral corruption the more dangerous epidemic.

Today: avoid one small hypocrisy you'd usually let slide.
meditations-9.3:
Don't scorn death, Marcus says, but welcome it as one of the things nature wills. Like growing up, getting teeth, a beard and gray hair, conceiving, giving birth and all of life's seasons, dissolution is natural. A thoughtful person waits for it without carelessness, impatience or contempt.

As you wait for a child to be born, wait for your soul to leave its shell.

If you want a more ordinary comfort, think about what you'll leave behind: people whose principles differ from yours. You should care for them gently, but the only thing that could make you cling to life would be living among people who share your values. Seeing how much friction there is, you might say, 'Come quickly, death, before I forget myself too.'

Today: be patient with one person whose values differ from yours.
meditations-9.4:
Whoever does wrong, Marcus says, wrongs himself. Whoever acts unjustly is unjust to himself, because he makes himself bad.

The Stoic view is that wrongdoing damages the wrongdoer most. Others may suffer losses, but the person who acts badly loses something more important: their character.

Today: when tempted to do something petty, remember who it would really harm.
meditations-9.5:
People often act unjustly by not doing something, Marcus says, not only by doing something.

It's an important point about responsibility. Failing to help, to speak up, or to do your part can be as wrong as active harm. Injustice includes neglect.

Today: do one thing you know you should do but have been avoiding.
meditations-9.6:
Your present judgment, grounded in understanding, Marcus says; your present action, aimed at the common good; and your present acceptance of everything that happens: that's enough.

Three things, all in the present: clear thinking, helpful action and acceptance. Marcus says nothing more is needed for a good life. It's a compact checklist you can apply to any moment.

Today: check yourself once against all three.
meditations-9.7:
Wipe out imagination, Marcus says. Check impulse. Quench desire. Keep your ruling faculty in your own power.

Four short commands, almost like a breathing exercise for the mind. Each one removes something that pulls you off balance, so that your judgment stays yours.

Today: when you feel pulled, try his four steps in order.
meditations-9.8:
Among animals without reason, Marcus says, one life is shared out. Among reasoning beings, one intelligent soul is shared out, just as there's one earth for all earthly things, and we all see by one light and breathe one air.

It's an image of deep kinship. Your reason isn't private property but a share in something common, like light or air. That's why human fellowship runs so deep.

Today: notice something you share with everyone around you, and treat them accordingly.
enchiridion-36:
In logic, Epictetus says, 'either it is day or it is night' works in an either-or argument but not in a combined one. Likewise, at a dinner, taking the biggest portion makes sense for your appetite but not for the spirit of the occasion. When you eat with others, remember not just what the food is worth to your body, but what courtesy you owe your host.

The logic analogy is a bit obscure, but the point is clear: what's good for you alone isn't always fitting in company. Context changes what's right.

Today: at a shared meal or moment, think about what's fitting for everyone, not just you.
meditations-9.9:
Everything that shares a common nature, Marcus says, moves toward its kind. Earth falls to earth, water flows together, fire rises and catches easily. Living things are even more drawn together: bees swarm, cattle herd, birds raise their young, animals form loves.

Rational beings go further still: communities, friendships, families, assemblies, even treaties in war. And the highest things, like the stars, are united even when far apart.

Yet humans alone seem to have forgotten this pull. Still, try as they might to separate, their nature is too strong. You'd sooner find a clod of earth touching nothing earthy than a person completely cut off from others.

Today: reach out to someone you've been keeping at a distance.
meditations-9.10:
Humans, God and the universe all bear fruit, Marcus says, each in its season. We usually use the word for vines and the like, but that doesn't matter. Reason bears fruit for everyone and for itself, producing more things like itself.

Good thinking produces more good thinking, both in you and in others. It's a quiet encouragement that wisdom spreads and multiplies.

Today: share one good idea with someone else.
meditations-9.11:
If you can, correct wrongdoers by teaching them, Marcus says. If you can't, remember that patience was given to you for exactly this. The gods are patient with such people too, and even help them get health, wealth and reputation, so kind are they. You can be too. Who's stopping you?

It's a gentle argument for tolerance. If the gods don't withhold good things from people who err, why should you withhold patience?

Today: be patient with someone you can't change.
meditations-9.12:
Don't work like someone miserable, Marcus says, or like someone wanting pity or admiration. Aim your will at one thing only: to act and to hold back as social reason requires.

It's a clean motivation for work. Not suffering, not seeking sympathy or applause, just doing what reason and the common good require.

Today: do your work without complaining or wanting credit.
meditations-9.13:
Today I got out of all my troubles, Marcus says, or rather I threw them out, because they weren't outside; they were inside, in my opinions.

The correction in the middle of the sentence is the lesson. He first says he escaped trouble, then realizes the trouble was never external. It was in how he was judging things, and so it was his to discard.

Today: pick one trouble and ask whether it's in the event or in your opinion of it.
meditations-9.14:
Everything is the same, Marcus says: familiar in experience, brief in time, worthless in substance. Everything now is as it was in the days of those we've buried.

It's a deflating observation, meant to cut down excitement and anxiety alike. Nothing is truly new or uniquely important. Seeing that clearly makes it easier to stay calm.

Today: when something feels unprecedented, remember people have faced versions of it for millennia.
meditations-9.15:
Things stand outside us, Marcus says, on their own, knowing nothing about themselves and making no judgment. What judges them, then? The ruling faculty.

Events don't come labeled 'good' or 'bad'. You supply the label. That's both a responsibility and a freedom: the verdict is yours to give, and yours to revise.

Today: when you label something a disaster, remember who did the labeling.
meditations-9.16:
The good and evil of a rational, social being lie not in what happens to them, Marcus says, but in what they do, just as their virtue and vice lie in action, not in passivity.

It's a clear statement of where to look. What befalls you doesn't make you good or bad. What you do with it does.

Today: measure your day by what you did, not by what happened to you.
meditations-9.17:
For a stone thrown into the air, Marcus says, it's no evil to come down, and no good to have been carried up.

A single, clear image. The stone's rise and fall are just physics, not triumph and disaster. Applied to life, it suggests our ups and downs might matter less than we think.

Today: treat one high and one low in your life with the same calm.
enchiridion-37:
If you take on a role beyond your strength, Epictetus says, you not only do it badly, but you also abandon one you could have filled well.

It's practical humility. Overreaching costs twice: the failure in the role you couldn't handle, and the loss of the good you could have done in a role that fit you.

Today: consider whether you've taken on something beyond you, and what you're neglecting because of it.
meditations-9.18:
Look into people's guiding principles, Marcus says, and you'll see what judges you fear, and what kind of judges they are of themselves.

Once you see how confused or self-critical many of your critics are, their opinions lose their sting. People who can't judge themselves well are unlikely to judge you well either.

Today: think of a critic you fear, and consider how they judge themselves.
meditations-9.19:
Everything is changing, Marcus says. You yourself are in constant change, and in a sense constant destruction, and so is the whole universe.

It's a bracing reminder that you're not a fixed thing watching change from outside. You're part of the flow. Cells die and renew, opinions shift, and the self that worries today isn't quite the self of tomorrow.

Today: notice one way you've changed recently, and accept it.
meditations-9.20:
Your job, Marcus says, is to leave another person's wrong where it is.

We tend to carry other people's misdeeds around: replaying them, resenting them, retelling them. Marcus says to leave them with the person who did them. They're not yours to carry.

Today: put down one grievance you've been carrying.
meditations-9.21:
The end of an activity, a pause in movement or opinion, is in a sense a death, Marcus says, and it isn't bad. Think of your life as a child, a youth, an adult, an old man: each change was a kind of death. Was that something to fear?

Think of your life under your grandfather, then your mother, then your father. You'll find many differences, changes and endings. Were they to be feared? Then neither is the ending of your whole life.

It's a gentle argument: you've already survived many endings of earlier selves.

Today: look back at a past version of yourself and notice that its ending wasn't a tragedy.
meditations-9.22:
Hurry to examine three minds, Marcus says. Your own, to make it just. The universe's, to remember what you're part of. Your neighbor's, to know whether they acted in ignorance or knowingly, and to remember their mind is akin to yours.

It's a compact practice of attention: improve yourself, place yourself in the larger order, and understand others with kinship rather than suspicion.

Today: spend a moment on each of the three.
meditations-9.23:
Just as you're part of a social system, Marcus says, let every act be part of social life. Any act that has no connection, near or distant, to the common good splits your life apart and stops it being whole. It's a kind of mutiny, like a man in an assembly standing apart from everyone's agreement.

The image of mutiny is strong. Acting only for yourself isn't neutral; it breaks the coherence of your life and your community.

Today: connect one ordinary task to someone else's good.
meditations-9.24:
Children's squabbles and games, Marcus says, and little souls carrying corpses around: that's everything. So the scenes of the underworld in poetry hit us more clearly.

'Little souls carrying corpses' echoes Epictetus's line about us being souls hauling bodies. The comparison to children's games is meant to puncture adult self-importance.

Today: look at one serious-seeming conflict as if it were a children's quarrel.
meditations-9.25:
Examine the form of a thing, Marcus says, separate it entirely from its material, and contemplate it. Then work out the longest time something of that form is naturally made to last.

It's an analytical exercise: see what something essentially is, and how long it can endure. Both tend to reduce its hold on you.

Today: analyze one thing you're attached to: what is it, really, and how long will it last?
meditations-9.26:
You've endured endless trouble, Marcus says, because you weren't content with your ruling faculty doing what it was made to do. But enough of that.

The last phrase is the point: a decision to stop. Much suffering comes from wanting more than your mind's proper work: wanting control over outcomes, others' opinions or circumstances. Marcus resolves to drop it.

Today: say 'enough' to one source of trouble you've been feeding.
enchiridion-38:
When you walk, Epictetus says, you take care not to step on a nail or twist your ankle. In the same way, take care not to injure your mind. If we guarded it like that in every action, we'd act more safely.

We instinctively protect our bodies from small injuries. Epictetus asks for the same care with our judgment: watching where our thoughts step.

Today: be as careful with your judgments as you are with your footing.
meditations-9.27:
When someone blames you, hates you or says something hurtful, Marcus says, go into their poor souls and see what kind of people they are. You'll find there's no reason to worry about their opinion of you.

But you should still be well disposed to them, for by nature they're your friends. The gods help them too, through dreams and signs, toward the things they value.

It's a double move: understanding critics drains their power, and remembering kinship keeps you kind.

Today: when someone criticizes you, consider what's going on inside them.
meditations-9.28:
The cycles of the universe repeat, Marcus says. Either universal reason acts deliberately for each event, in which case accept its results; or it acted once, and everything follows from that; or atoms are the origin of everything. In short: if there's a god, all is well; if chance rules, don't you be ruled by chance.

Soon the earth will cover us all, then change itself, and its products will keep changing forever. Watching the waves of change and their speed, you'll despise everything perishable.

The key line is: 'if chance rules, don't you be governed by it.' Even in a random world, you can act with reason.

Today: in one chaotic situation, act deliberately anyway.
meditations-9.29:
The universe is like a winter torrent, Marcus says, sweeping everything along. And how worthless are these little people in politics who think they're playing the philosopher. Drivellers.

So do what nature asks now. Act, if you can, without looking around to see who's watching. Don't expect Plato's ideal Republic; be content if the smallest thing goes well, and don't think that small. Who can change people's opinions? Without that, you only get slaves who groan while pretending to obey.

As for Alexander, Philip and Demetrius, let them answer for themselves. If they were tragic posturers, no one has condemned me to imitate them. Philosophy's work is simple and modest.

Today: be content with one small thing going well.
meditations-9.30:
Look down from above, Marcus says, at the countless herds of people, their ceremonies, their voyages in storm and calm, the variety of those born, living together and dying. Think of lives lived long ago, lives to come, and lives among distant peoples. How many don't know your name, how many will soon forget it, and how those who praise you now may soon blame you.

Neither posthumous fame, nor reputation, nor anything of that kind is worth anything.

It's another 'view from above', meant to shrink the importance of being known.

Today: picture your worries from high above, among billions of other lives.
meditations-9.31:
Toward what comes from outside, Marcus says, be undisturbed. In what you do from within, be just: let your impulses and actions end in acts that serve others, as is natural for you.

It's a two-part summary of Stoic ethics. Accept what you can't control calmly; make what you can control fair and helpful.

Today: accept one external event calmly, and do one fair, helpful act.
meditations-9.32:
You can remove many useless things that disturb you, Marcus says, because they exist only in your opinion. Then you'll give yourself a lot of room: by taking in the whole universe in your mind, contemplating eternity, and noticing how fast each thing changes, how short the time from birth to dissolution, and how vast the time before birth and after it.

It's an invitation to make space in your mind by enlarging your view. Small worries crowd you only when your perspective is small.

Today: when something crowds your mind, zoom out until it has room.
meditations-9.33:
Everything you see will soon perish, Marcus says, and those who watch it perish will soon perish too. Whoever dies at a great age ends up in the same state as someone who died young.

It's one of his recurring levellers. Length of life doesn't change the destination. That's meant to make you focus on how you live, not how long.

Today: spend one hour as if its quality mattered more than its length.
meditations-9.34:
What are these people's guiding principles, Marcus asks? What do they busy themselves with? Why do they love and honor what they do? Imagine their poor souls laid bare. When they think they're doing harm by blaming or good by praising, what an idea!

Seeing people's motives clearly shrinks the power of their opinions. Praise and blame from confused minds are less weighty than they feel.

Today: when praise or blame lands on you, ask what's behind it.
meditations-9.35:
Loss is nothing but change, Marcus says, and nature delights in change. Everything happens well by her order, has always been like this and always will be. So what are you saying: that everything always was and always will be bad, that none of the gods could ever fix it, and the world is condemned to endless evil?

The question exposes the implications of constant complaint. If loss is just change, then calling it evil means calling the whole universe evil.

Today: reframe one loss as a change rather than a catastrophe.
meditations-9.36:
The decay underlying everything, Marcus says: water, dust, bones, filth. Marble is a hardened lump of earth; gold and silver are sediments; clothes are bits of hair; purple dye is blood. Everything else is the same. Even breath is just the same stuff changing from one form to another.

It's a deliberately unromantic look at what things are made of, meant to strip away the glamour of luxury and status.

Today: look at one luxury item and describe what it's actually made of.
enchiridion-39:
The body is the measure of what you need to own, Epictetus says, as the foot is the measure of the shoe. Stay with that, and you keep the right measure. Go past it, and you'll be carried as if over a cliff. With a shoe, once it's more than the foot needs, it becomes gilded, then purple, then studded with jewels. Once you exceed the proper measure, there's no limit.

It's a clear picture of how wants escalate. 'Enough' is a natural stopping point; beyond it, there isn't one.

Today: notice one possession or desire that has passed the point of need.
meditations-9.37:
Enough of this miserable life, Marcus says, the grumbling and monkey tricks. Why are you upset? What's new here? What's unsettling you? The form of the thing? Look at it. The material? Look at it. There's nothing else. So turn to the gods, and at last become simpler and better. Examining these things for a hundred years or three makes no difference.

It's an impatient pep talk to himself. When something disturbs you, look at what it actually is, and you'll usually find nothing that justifies the fuss.

Today: when something rattles you, look at it closely and ask what exactly is upsetting.
meditations-9.38:
If someone has done wrong, Marcus says, the harm is theirs. But perhaps they haven't done wrong.

Two short sentences, two useful moves. First, wrongdoing mostly harms the wrongdoer. Second, check your assumption: you may have misjudged them. Both cool anger quickly.

Today: when you think someone has wronged you, consider that you might be mistaken.
meditations-9.39:
Either everything comes from one intelligent source and fits together like one body, Marcus says, in which case the part shouldn't complain about what's done for the whole; or there are only atoms, mixing and scattering. So why are you upset?

Ask your mind: are you dead? Corrupted? Pretending? Turned beast? Herding and grazing with the rest?

His usual either-or leads to calm. Then the sharper questions check whether you've lost your humanity in reacting.

Today: when agitated, ask whether you're acting like a thinking person or a herd animal.
meditations-9.40:
Either the gods have power or they don't, Marcus says. If not, why pray? If so, why not pray to be free from fear, desire and grief, rather than praying for things to happen or not happen?

'But the gods put those things in my power.' Then isn't it better to use your power freely than to crave what isn't in your power like a slave? And who says the gods don't help with what's in our power?

So change your prayers. Not 'how can I have that woman?' but 'how can I stop wanting her?' Not 'how can I be rid of this?' but 'how can I stop needing to be rid of it?' Not 'how can I not lose my son?' but 'how can I not fear losing him?'

Today: turn one wish about circumstances into a wish about your own response.
meditations-9.41:
Marcus quotes Epicurus, a rival philosopher, describing his illness: he didn't talk about his bodily suffering, but kept discussing nature and how the mind can stay calm while the body hurts. He didn't let the doctors act self-important; his life went on well and happily.

Do the same, Marcus says, in sickness and in everything. Every school of philosophy agrees: don't abandon philosophy when things happen, don't waste time on idle talk, and focus on what you're doing now and the tool you're doing it with.

It's generous of a Stoic to take a lesson from an Epicurean. Good examples can come from anywhere.

Today: if you're unwell or struggling, talk about something other than your troubles.
meditations-9.42:
When someone's shamelessness offends you, Marcus says, ask: is it possible for there to be no shameless people in the world? No. So don't demand the impossible. This is just one of them. Do the same with cheats, the faithless and every wrongdoer. Remembering such people must exist will make you kinder to each one.

Nature gave us virtues to counter each fault: gentleness against stupidity, and so on. You can always try to teach someone who's gone astray. And how have you been harmed? None of them has made your mind worse.

If you're shocked that someone ungrateful was ungrateful, blame yourself for expecting otherwise. And when you do good, don't want payment. That's like the eye asking a fee for seeing.

Today: help someone with no expectation of thanks.
meditations-10.1:
Marcus addresses his own soul. Will you ever be good, simple, whole and transparent, plainer than the body around you? Will you ever be affectionate and content, full, wanting nothing, not longing for pleasure, more time, a better place, a nicer climate or more agreeable company?

Will you ever be satisfied with your present state, pleased with everything around you, convinced you have everything you need from the gods, and that all is and will be well?

Will you ever live with gods and people in such a way that you neither find fault with them nor are condemned by them?

It's a yearning, almost a prayer, for the contentment he keeps striving toward.

Today: spend a few minutes being content with exactly what you have.
meditations-10.2:
Notice what your nature needs as a living thing, Marcus says, and do it, as long as it doesn't make you worse as an animal. Then notice what you need as an animal, and allow it, as long as it doesn't make you worse as a rational being. And a rational being is also a social being. Use these rules and don't trouble yourself about anything else.

It's a layered approach to needs. Meet bodily and animal needs, but never at the expense of reason, and reason includes caring for others.

Today: check one bodily want against whether it makes you less thoughtful or less kind.
meditations-10.3:
Everything that happens is either something you're made to bear or something you're not, Marcus says. If you're made to bear it, don't complain; bear it. If you're not, don't complain either; it will consume you and then end.

But remember: you're made to bear everything that your own opinion can make bearable, by thinking of it as in your interest or your duty.

It's a bracing argument. Most things are bearable once you see them as duty or as useful. And those that aren't won't last long.

Today: reframe one hard thing as a duty or an opportunity.
enchiridion-40:
From the age of fourteen, Epictetus says, girls are flattered by men as 'ladies'. Seeing that they're valued only for giving men pleasure, they start adorning themselves and put all their hopes in that. So it's worth helping them see they're honored only for being modest and well-behaved.

The passage reflects the attitudes of its time and reads awkwardly now. But the underlying criticism holds: a society that values people mainly for their looks teaches them to invest everything in appearance. Epictetus wants worth to rest on character instead.

Today: compliment someone on their character rather than their appearance.
meditations-10.4:
If someone is mistaken, Marcus says, teach them kindly and show them their error. If you can't, blame yourself, or not even yourself.

It's a gentle progression. First try to help. If that fails, consider whether you could have done better. And then, if no one's at fault, let it go without blame at all.

Today: correct one mistake kindly, or let it go without blame.
meditations-10.5:
Whatever happens to you, Marcus says, was prepared for you from all eternity. The chain of causes was spinning your existence, and everything that would befall you, from the beginning.

This is Stoic fate. It can sound fatalistic, but Marcus uses it as consolation: what happens isn't random cruelty, but part of a long, coherent unfolding.

Today: treat one event as part of a long chain rather than a personal attack.
meditations-10.6:
Whether the universe is atoms or an ordered nature, Marcus says, let this be settled first: I'm part of a whole governed by nature, and I'm closely related to other parts of my kind.

Because I'm a part, I won't resent anything assigned to me from the whole, since nothing that benefits the whole harms the part. Because I'm related to others like me, I'll do nothing antisocial, and I'll direct my efforts toward the common good.

Then life will flow happily, like a citizen who works for his fellow citizens and accepts whatever the city assigns him.

Today: do one thing that helps your community, and accept one thing it asks of you.
meditations-10.7:
Everything in the universe must perish, Marcus says, meaning it must change. If change were both bad and unavoidable for the parts, the whole couldn't stay in good condition. Did nature deliberately harm her own parts, or not notice? Both are absurd.

And it's ridiculous to say things naturally change and then be shocked when they do, especially since dissolution is just returning to what things were made of.

He adds that the body you have isn't even the one you were born with; it was built from food and air 'yesterday and the day before'. What changes is that, not your true self.

Today: when something changes, remember that change is its nature, not a betrayal.
meditations-10.8:
Once you've taken on the names good, modest, truthful, rational, even-tempered and great-souled, Marcus says, don't change them, and if you lose them, return quickly. Rational means careful attention to each thing. Even-tempered means willingly accepting what nature assigns. Great-souled means rising above pleasure, pain, fame and death.

Hold these names without needing others to call you by them, and you'll become a new person. Staying as you were is like the half-mauled arena fighters who beg to be kept alive for the next day's beasts.

If you can keep these names, live as if on the Isles of the Blessed. If you slip, find a quiet corner where you can keep them. Remember that what does a fig tree's work is a fig tree, and what does a human's work is a human.

Today: choose one of his names and live up to it today.
meditations-10.9:
Farce, war, shock, sluggishness and servitude, Marcus says, will wear away your principles day by day. How much do you imagine without studying nature, and how much do you neglect?

Your duty is to see and do everything so that your practical skill grows, your reflection is exercised, and the confidence that comes from understanding is kept, not shown off but not hidden either.

When will you enjoy simplicity, seriousness and understanding what each thing is, its place in the universe, how long it lasts, what it's made of, and who can give it or take it away?

Today: notice one distraction wearing down your principles, and push back.
meditations-10.10:
A spider is proud of catching a fly, Marcus says. One man is proud of catching a hare, another a fish, another wild boars, another bears, another Sarmatians. Aren't they all robbers, if you look at their principles?

The twist is that Marcus himself was fighting the Sarmatians on the Danube frontier. He's turning a harsh eye on his own victories, comparing military glory to a spider's catch.

Today: look honestly at one thing you're proud of, and ask what it really is.
meditations-10.11:
Learn to see how everything changes into everything else, Marcus says, and keep practicing this. Nothing builds greatness of mind like it. Such a person has, in a sense, put off the body. Knowing he must soon leave everything, he gives himself wholly to acting justly and accepting what nature brings.

What others say, think or do against him doesn't even occur to him. He's content with two things: acting justly now, and accepting what's assigned now. He drops distracting busyness and wants only to go straight along the path of law, and so follow God.

Today: be content with acting justly and accepting what comes.
meditations-10.12:
Why be anxious and suspicious, Marcus asks, when you can simply work out what should be done? If you see clearly, go that way contentedly, without turning back. If you don't see clearly, stop and consult the best advisers. If other things get in the way, go on as best you can, carefully, keeping to what seems just.

It's best to succeed in that. If you fail, let your failure be in the attempt.

Someone who follows reason is calm and active at once, cheerful and composed.

Today: when unsure, ask for good advice rather than worrying alone.
enchiridion-41:
It's a sign of a dull mind, Epictetus says, to spend a lot of time on bodily things: overdoing exercise, eating, drinking and other animal functions. These should be done in passing, with our main effort given to the mind.

He isn't against health or exercise; he's against obsession with the body at the expense of the mind. Bodily care is maintenance, not the main project.

Today: spend a little less attention on your body and a little more on your thinking.
meditations-10.13:
As soon as you wake, Marcus says, ask yourself: will it make any difference to me if someone else does what's just and right? None.

Then: surely you haven't forgotten that people who pompously praise or blame others are the same people at bed and at table, with their habits, pursuits and thefts, not with hands and feet, but with their most precious part, which could produce loyalty, modesty, truth, law and happiness.

The first point is a morning check on envy and rivalry. The second deflates the people whose judgments we fear.

Today: when someone else does well, let it make no difference to your peace.
meditations-10.14:
To nature, who gives and takes back everything, Marcus says, the educated and modest person says: give what you will, take back what you will. And he says it not defiantly, but obediently and gladly.

The tone matters. It's not grim resignation or proud defiance, but a cheerful trust. Life is on loan, and the borrower is grateful.

Today: let go of one thing gracefully, as though returning a loan.
meditations-10.15:
What's left of your life is short, Marcus says. Live as if on a mountain. It makes no difference whether you live here or there, if you live everywhere as a citizen of the world.

Let people see, let them know, a real human being living according to nature. If they can't bear him, let them kill him. That's better than living the way they do.

'Live as if on a mountain' suggests detachment and clarity: above the noise, wherever you are.

Today: live one hour as if above the noise around you.
meditations-10.16:
'No longer talk at all about what a good man should be. Be one.'

It's one of Marcus's most famous lines, and a rebuke to himself as much as anyone. Discussing virtue is easy and endless; practicing it is the point. The Meditations themselves are notes to himself, not lectures to others.

Today: stop thinking about one good thing you should do, and do it.
meditations-10.17:
Constantly contemplate all of time and all of substance, Marcus says, and see that each individual thing is, in substance, a fig seed, and in time, the turn of a drill.

The images are tiny and precise. A fig seed in the vastness of matter; a single twist of a gimlet in the span of eternity. It's another way of shrinking worries to their true size.

Today: when something feels overwhelming, picture it as a fig seed against the universe.
meditations-10.18:
Look at everything that exists, Marcus says, and see that it's already dissolving and changing, decaying or scattering, or that everything is made by nature to die.

It's a deliberately unsentimental exercise. Nothing is static; decay is already underway in everything. Seeing that makes attachments looser and losses less surprising.

Today: notice one thing that's slowly changing, and accept it.
meditations-10.19:
Think of what people are like when they're eating, sleeping, having sex, relieving themselves, Marcus says. Then think of them when they're imperious and arrogant, or angry and scolding from on high. Not long ago they were slaves to so many things, and soon they'll be in some sorry state again.

It's a leveling exercise for dealing with people who act superior. Everyone shares the same basic, humbling bodily needs.

Today: when someone acts superior, remember they're as human as you.
meditations-10.20:
What nature brings to each thing is good for it, Marcus says, and good at the time nature brings it.

It's a short statement of trust in timing. The Stoic view is that events arrive when they should. You don't have to agree fully to benefit from asking whether something might be right for this moment.

Today: consider whether one unwelcome event might be arriving at the right time.
meditations-10.21:
'The earth loves the rain,' the poet Euripides says, 'and the holy sky loves.' And the universe loves to make whatever is going to be. So I say to the universe: I love what you love.

Marcus plays on a Greek idiom in which 'loves to' also means 'tends to'. Things that 'love to happen' are things that usually happen. He chooses to love them too.

It's acceptance expressed as affection.

Today: find something to love in one thing that tends to happen.
meditations-10.22:
Either you live here and have got used to it, Marcus says; or you're leaving, and that was your choice; or you're dying, and you've done your duty. There's nothing beyond these. So cheer up.

It's a deliberately simple comfort. Every possibility is manageable: stay, go or end. None is a reason for despair.

Today: if you're dreading a situation, list the possible outcomes and notice none is unbearable.
enchiridion-42:
When someone treats you badly or speaks ill of you, Epictetus says, remember they think they're right to do it. They can't follow what seems right to you, only what seems right to them. If they judge wrongly, they're the ones harmed, because they're the ones deceived. If someone takes a true statement to be false, the statement isn't hurt; only the person is mistaken.

Starting from this, you'll be gentle with anyone who insults you, saying each time, 'It seemed so to him.'

Today: when someone misjudges you, say to yourself, 'It seemed right to them.'
meditations-10.23:
Always keep in mind, Marcus says, that this patch of land is like any other, and that everything here is the same as on a mountaintop, by the sea, or anywhere you'd like to be. You'll find what Plato says: living in a city is like living in a shepherd's fold on a mountain.

The longing for elsewhere is common. Marcus says it's an illusion. Wherever you are, the conditions for living well are the same.

Today: instead of wishing you were elsewhere, live well where you are.
meditations-10.24:
What is my ruling faculty to me right now? Marcus asks. What am I making it into? What am I using it for? Is it empty of understanding? Is it cut off from community? Is it melted into the flesh, moving with every bodily impulse?

It's a set of check-in questions you can actually use. They ask whether you're thinking clearly, connected to others, and in charge of your impulses.

Today: ask his questions at three points in your day.
meditations-10.25:
Someone who flees his master is a runaway, Marcus says. But the law is a master, and whoever breaks it is a runaway. So is anyone who's grieved, angry or afraid, because they resent something that has been, is, or will be ordained by the one who rules all, who is Law and gives each what's fitting.

It's a striking reframe. Grief, anger and fear are treated as a kind of desertion from the natural order. Accepting it is staying at your post.

Today: when you feel resentful, ask whether you're running from something you need to accept.
meditations-10.26:
A man deposits seed in a womb and leaves, Marcus says, and another cause takes over and makes a child. What a thing from such material! Then the child swallows food, and another cause turns it into perception, movement, life and strength. How many and how wonderful!

Watch these hidden processes, he says, and see the power behind them, just as we see the force that makes things fall or rise, not with our eyes, but just as clearly.

It's a moment of wonder at life's quiet processes.

Today: notice one ordinary process in your body or the world and appreciate it.
meditations-10.27:
Keep in mind how everything now was the same in the past, Marcus says, and will be again. Picture whole dramas and stages of the same form, from your experience or from history: the court of Hadrian, the court of Antoninus, the courts of Philip, Alexander and Croesus. All were the same plays we see now, with different actors.

It's a way of not taking the current drama too seriously. The cast changes; the plot is old.

Today: see one current drama as a rerun with new actors.
meditations-10.28:
Picture everyone who is grieved or discontented, Marcus says, as like a pig being sacrificed, kicking and squealing. So is the one who lies on his bed silently lamenting the chains we're all held by.

Only rational beings are given the power to follow events willingly. Simply following is forced on everyone.

The image is harsh, but the point is liberating. We all have to go along with what happens; we can choose to go willingly rather than kicking.

Today: go along willingly with one thing you'd usually resist.
meditations-10.29:
With each thing you do, Marcus says, pause and ask: is death terrible because it deprives me of this?

It's a powerful filter. Many of our activities wouldn't be missed. Asking this question reveals what really matters to you, and what you could let go.

Today: ask his question about three things you do.
meditations-10.30:
When someone's fault offends you, Marcus says, immediately turn to yourself and think how you go wrong in a similar way: thinking money is good, or pleasure, or a little fame.
