That will quickly cool your anger, especially if you add that the person is compelled. What else could they do? Or, if you can, free them from the compulsion.

It's an effective technique. Recognizing your own version of someone's fault turns judgment into fellow feeling.

Today: when someone annoys you, find your own version of their fault.
meditations-10.31:
When you see one person, Marcus says, think of someone similar who's dead. When you see Satyron the Socratic, think of Eutyches or Hymen; when you see the philosopher Euphrates, think of Eutychion or Silvanus. And when you look at yourself, think of any other Caesar. Then ask: where are they now? Nowhere, or nobody knows.

So human things are smoke. Why not pass through your short time in an orderly way? What are all these events but exercises for reason?

Keep at it until you make them your own, as a strong stomach digests everything, or a blazing fire turns everything into light.

Today: treat one difficulty as fuel for the fire rather than something to avoid.
enchiridion-43:
Everything has two handles, Epictetus says: one by which it can be carried, and one by which it can't. If your brother wrongs you, don't pick it up by the handle of his wrong, because that way it can't be carried. Pick it up by the other handle: he's your brother, raised with you. That way it can be carried.

It's one of the most practical images in the book. The same situation can be grasped in a way that makes it bearable or unbearable. You choose which handle.

Today: find the bearable handle on one difficult situation.
meditations-10.32:
Don't let anyone be able to say truthfully that you're not simple or not good, Marcus says. If anyone thinks that of you, let them be lying. That's entirely in your power. Who can stop you being good and simple? Just decide not to go on living unless you are.

The last line is intense, but the core idea is clear: your character is the one thing no one else controls. Make it so solid that any accusation against it is simply false.

Today: act so that no one could truthfully call you unkind.
meditations-10.33:
What's the most reasonable thing to do or say with the material in front of you? Marcus asks. Whatever it is, you can do it. Don't make excuses. You'll keep complaining until doing what fits your nature feels to you as luxury feels to pleasure-seekers.

Cylinders, water and fire are easily blocked, but reason can move through every obstacle, as fire rises and a stone falls. Obstacles affect only the body, or harm you only if reason gives way.

When other things are harmed they get worse; but a person who uses misfortune well becomes better. And nothing harms a citizen that doesn't harm the city, and nothing harms the city that doesn't harm law.

Today: find the most reasonable action in one situation and take it.
meditations-10.34:
For someone steeped in true principles, Marcus says, even a short line is enough to free them from grief and fear. For example, Homer: 'Leaves, the wind scatters some on the ground; so is the race of men.'

Your children are leaves. So are those who praise or curse you, and those who'll pass on your fame. They sprout in spring, the wind blows them down, and the forest grows new ones. Everything is brief, yet you chase and flee things as if they were eternal. Soon you'll close your eyes, and someone will mourn the one who mourned you.

It's one of the most beautiful and sober passages in the book.

Today: hold one person you love a little more gently, knowing life is brief.
meditations-10.35:
A healthy eye should see everything visible, Marcus says, not say 'I only want green things'; that's a sick eye. Healthy hearing and smell should take in everything. A healthy stomach should handle all food, as a mill grinds whatever it's made to grind.

So a healthy mind should be ready for whatever happens. The mind that says 'let my children live, let everyone praise me' is like an eye that wants only green, or teeth that want only soft food.

It's a tough but clarifying image: resilience means being able to take what comes, not only what you'd prefer.

Today: meet one unwelcome thing as a healthy mind would.
meditations-10.36:
No one is so fortunate, Marcus says, that no one at his deathbed will be glad. Even a good, wise man will have someone thinking, 'At last we can breathe, free of this schoolmaster. He was never harsh, but I felt he silently judged us.'

And in my case there are many more reasons people would want me gone. Remember this when dying, and you'll go more contentedly: even those I worked and prayed for may want me to leave.

But don't leave less kindly toward them. Stay friendly, generous and gentle, and go not as if torn away, but as a soul slips easily from the body in a peaceful death.

Today: be kind to someone who might not appreciate you.
meditations-10.37:
Whenever someone does something, Marcus says, practice asking: what is this person aiming at? But start with yourself, and examine yourself first.

Asking about motives builds understanding of others. Starting with your own motives keeps you honest and humble.

Today: before judging someone's motive, examine your own in a similar moment.
meditations-10.38:
Remember that what pulls the strings is hidden inside, Marcus says: the power of persuasion, life, in a sense the person. When you think about yourself, don't include the body around you and its attached organs. They're like an axe, except that they grow on you. Without the cause that moves and restrains them, they're no more useful than a weaver's shuttle, a writer's pen or a driver's whip.

The real you is the mind that directs; the body is the tool.

Today: pay attention to what's directing your actions, not just the actions themselves.
meditations-11.1:
Marcus lists the properties of the rational soul. It sees itself, analyses itself and shapes itself as it chooses. It enjoys its own fruit, unlike plants, whose fruit others enjoy. It reaches its goal wherever life ends. Unlike a dance or a play, cut short and incomplete, it makes each moment full and complete, so it can say, 'I have what is mine.'

It travels the whole universe, surveys its form, reaches into infinite time and grasps the cycles of renewal, realizing that someone of forty, if they understand anything, has seen all that was and will be.

It also loves its neighbor, values truth and modesty, and ranks nothing above itself, which is the property of law. Right reason and justice are the same.

Today: make one ordinary moment complete in itself.
meditations-11.2:
You'll value songs, dances and the pancratium, a brutal combat sport, much less, Marcus says, if you break them into parts. Divide a melody into its individual notes and ask whether you're mastered by each one; you'd be ashamed to say yes. Do the same with each movement of a dance, and with the fighting.

In everything except virtue and its acts, break things into their parts and value them less that way. Apply this to your whole life too.

It's a technique for loosening the grip of enthusiasms: analysis drains glamour.

Today: break one thing you're overly attached to into its parts.
enchiridion-44:
These arguments don't follow, Epictetus says: 'I'm richer than you, so I'm better than you.' 'I'm more eloquent than you, so I'm better than you.' What follows is: 'I'm richer, so my property is greater.' 'I'm more eloquent, so my speech is better.' But you aren't your property or your speech.

It's a precise logical correction. Advantages in possessions or skills don't make one person better than another. Worth lies in character.

Today: catch yourself ranking someone above or below you because of what they have.
meditations-11.3:
What a soul, Marcus says, that is ready, whenever it must leave the body, to be extinguished, scattered, or continue to exist. But this readiness should come from its own judgment, not sheer obstinacy, as with the Christians, but thoughtfully, with dignity, and persuasively, without theatrics.

This is the only mention of Christians in the Meditations, and some scholars think it was added later. Marcus is contrasting reasoned calm about death with what he saw as stubborn martyrdom.

The point for us is the kind of courage he values: calm and reasoned, not dramatic.

Today: face one fear with calm reasoning rather than bravado.
meditations-11.4:
Have I done something for the common good? Marcus asks. Then I've had my reward. Keep this in mind always, and never stop.

The reward for doing good is having done it. Not recognition, not repayment. That makes generosity self-sustaining: you don't need anything else to keep going.

Today: do something for the common good and count that as the reward.
meditations-11.5:
What is your craft? Marcus asks. To be good. And how is that done well, except through general principles: some about the nature of the universe, others about the proper makeup of human beings?

It's a reminder that being good isn't just a mood; it's a skill, and skills rest on understanding. Stoics studied nature and human nature so they could live well.

Today: learn one thing about how people or the world work that would help you act better.
meditations-11.6:
Tragedy was first staged, Marcus says, to remind people of what happens in life, that it's natural, and that if you enjoy it on stage you shouldn't be troubled on the larger stage. Even those who cry out 'O Cithaeron!', as Oedipus does, have to bear it. Some lines are worth remembering, like 'Me and my children if the gods neglect, this has its reason too,' 'We must not chafe and fret at that which happens,' and 'Life's harvest reap like the wheat's fruitful ear.'

Then came the old comedy, with its frank speech, useful for puncturing arrogance; Diogenes used to borrow from it. But the middle and new comedy slid into mere clever imitation. What is all that for?

It's a short history of theater judged by whether it teaches you to live.

Today: take one lesson from a story you've enjoyed.
meditations-11.7:
How obvious it is, Marcus says, that no condition of life is better suited for doing philosophy than the one you're in right now.

From an emperor at war, it's a striking claim. There's no ideal situation for becoming wise. Your present circumstances, with all their difficulties, are exactly the material you have to work with.

Today: practice one principle in your current situation rather than waiting for a better one.
meditations-11.8:
A branch cut from the next branch is cut from the whole tree, Marcus says. So a person separated from another has fallen away from the whole community. A branch is cut by someone else, but a person cuts himself off by hating and turning away, not realizing he's cut himself from all of society.

Yet Zeus gave us the gift of being able to grow back and rejoin the whole. But if it happens often, it becomes harder to reunite. And a branch that has always grown with the tree isn't quite like one cut off and grafted back; gardeners say it grows with the tree but doesn't share its mind.

It's a tender passage about estrangement and reconciliation, and the cost of repeated breaks.

Today: mend one small rift before it grows.
meditations-11.9:
Those who try to block you when you're acting rightly can't turn you from your course, Marcus says. So don't let them drive you from goodwill toward them either. Guard both: steady judgment and action, and gentleness toward those who obstruct or annoy you.

Being angry at them is a weakness, just like being diverted from your path or giving in out of fear. Both desert their post: one through fear, the other by turning against a natural kinsman and friend.

It's a balanced ideal: firm in action, gentle in attitude.

Today: stay firm with someone who opposes you, and stay kind.
meditations-11.10:
No nature is inferior to art, Marcus says, because arts imitate nature. So the most perfect and complete nature can't fall short of art. All crafts make lower things for the sake of higher ones, so nature does too.

That's the origin of justice, and justice is the foundation of the other virtues. But justice can't survive if we care about things that don't matter, or are easily fooled, careless or fickle.

The chain of reasoning ends in something practical: justice requires not being distracted by trivial goods.

Today: make one fair decision without being swayed by something trivial.
meditations-11.11:
If the things whose pursuit or avoidance disturbs you aren't coming to you, Marcus says, then in a sense you're going to them. So let your judgment about them rest, and they'll stay quiet, and you won't be seen chasing or fleeing them.

It's a subtle insight: we often create our own disturbances by mentally reaching for or recoiling from things that aren't even present.

Today: notice one thing you're mentally chasing or fleeing that isn't actually in front of you.
meditations-11.12:
The soul keeps its spherical shape, Marcus says, when it doesn't stretch toward any object, shrink inward, scatter or sink, but is lit by the light by which it sees the truth: the truth of everything, and the truth within itself.

The sphere was an old image, from the philosopher Empedocles, for perfect completeness. A mind in that state isn't grasping, cowering or dissipating. It's whole, balanced and clear-sighted.

Today: notice whether your mind is grasping, shrinking or scattered, and bring it back to balance.
enchiridion-45:
Does someone bathe quickly? Epictetus asks. Don't say they bathe badly, just quickly. Does someone drink a lot of wine? Don't say they act badly, just that they drink a lot. Unless you understand their reasons, how do you know they're doing wrong? This way you won't assent to impressions you don't fully understand.

It's a discipline of description. Separate what you observe from your judgment of it. Most snap judgments add a verdict the facts don't support.

Today: describe one person's behavior without adding a judgment.
meditations-11.13:
Someone despises me? Marcus says. That's their business. Mine is to make sure I'm never caught doing or saying anything that deserves contempt. Someone hates me? Their business. I'll be gentle and kind to everyone, ready to show even that person their mistake, not reproachfully or as a display of patience, but honestly, like the great Phocion, if he really meant it.

Phocion was an Athenian statesman famous for integrity, who, condemned to death, reportedly asked his son to bear the Athenians no grudge.

Your inner life should be such that the gods see you neither discontented nor complaining.

Today: when someone dislikes you, focus only on whether you've earned it.
meditations-11.14:
People despise each other and flatter each other, Marcus says. They want to rise above one another, and they grovel before one another.

It's a compact picture of social life's contradictions: contempt and flattery, ambition and servility, often in the same people. Seeing the pattern clearly helps you step out of it.

Today: notice when you're tempted to look down on someone or to flatter them, and do neither.
meditations-11.15:
How false, Marcus says, is the person who announces, 'I've decided to deal fairly with you.' What are you doing? No need to announce it. It will show in your actions. It should be written on your forehead. Character shows immediately in the eyes, as a lover reads everything in the eyes of the beloved.

A good, honest person should be like someone who smells strongly: anyone nearby notices, whether they want to or not. But fake simplicity is like a crooked stick. Nothing is more shameful than a wolf's friendship. Avoid it above all.

Today: let one good intention show in action instead of announcing it.
meditations-11.16:
The power to live well is in the soul, Marcus says, if it's indifferent to things that don't matter. It will be, if it looks at each of them separately and as a whole, and remembers that none of them forms an opinion about itself or comes to us. They stay put. We form the judgments and, so to speak, write them on ourselves. We can choose not to write them, and if they've slipped in, we can wipe them out.

And this attention is only needed for a short time; then life is over.

If something fits nature, enjoy it; if not, seek what fits your nature, even without reputation.

Today: erase one judgment you've written on yourself about something outside your control.
meditations-11.17:
Consider where each thing comes from, Marcus says, what it's made of, what it changes into, what it will be after the change, and that it will suffer no harm.

It's a short analytic exercise for loosening attachment. Things come from somewhere, are made of something, and become something else. Change isn't harm; it's just transformation.

Today: trace one thing you value from its origin to its eventual change.
meditations-11.18:
The longest passage in the book: nine rules, plus a tenth, for when someone offends you.

One: remember we're made for one another. Two: think of what people are like at home, and what beliefs compel them. Three: if they act rightly, don't be upset; if wrongly, they do it unwillingly, out of ignorance. Four: you do plenty wrong too, and you avoid some faults only out of fear or vanity. Five: you may not even know they're wrong; you'd need to know much more.

Six: life is brief; soon we're all dead. Seven: it isn't their actions that disturb you but your judgments; drop those and the anger goes. Eight: anger hurts you more than the act did. Nine: real kindness is invincible. Correct them gently, privately: 'Not so, my child; you're only harming yourself.'

And a tenth, from Apollo: expecting bad people never to do wrong is madness. But letting them wrong others while expecting them to spare you is tyrannical.

Gentleness, he concludes, is strength; anger is weakness.

Today: when someone offends you, try one of the nine.
meditations-11.19:
Watch for four distortions of the mind, Marcus says, and when you catch them, wipe them out. For each, say: 'This thought isn't necessary.' 'This one undermines community.' 'This isn't what I really think,' since speaking against your real thoughts is absurd. And the fourth is reproaching yourself, a sign that the divine part in you is being overpowered by the body and its pleasures.

The four filters are useful: is it necessary, is it social, is it sincere, and is it a sign I've let my lower self win?

Today: run one thought through his four filters.
meditations-11.20:
The airy and fiery parts of you naturally rise, Marcus says, yet they're held down in your body by the order of the universe. The earthy and watery parts naturally fall, yet they're held up. The elements obey their place until the signal comes for dissolution.

Isn't it strange, then, that only your intelligence should rebel against its place, when nothing is forced on it except what fits its nature? Moving toward injustice, excess, anger, grief or fear is deviating from nature. So is resenting what happens, since the mind is made for reverence as well as justice.

The elements quietly accept their position. Why can't the mind?

Today: accept one aspect of your situation as the elements accept theirs.
meditations-11.21:
Whoever doesn't have one consistent aim in life, Marcus says, can't be one consistent person. But that's not enough without saying what the aim should be. People don't agree about all the things they call good, only about some, the ones that serve the common good. So we should choose an aim that's social and civic. Whoever directs all their efforts there will make all their actions consistent, and will always be the same person.

It's a recipe for integrity in the literal sense: being whole. A single social purpose unifies a life.

Today: name your main aim in one sentence, and check one action against it.
enchiridion-46:
Never call yourself a philosopher, Epictetus says, or talk much about your principles among people who don't share them. Show them in action. At a dinner, don't lecture people on how to eat; eat as you should. Socrates avoided all showing off. When people asked him to introduce them to philosophers, he did, and bore being overlooked.

If principles come up among the uninformed, mostly stay silent; it's risky to spit out what you haven't digested. If someone says you know nothing and it doesn't sting, you've really begun.

Sheep don't vomit up grass to show the shepherd how much they ate. They digest it and produce wool and milk. Show your principles the same way: by what they produce in your actions.

Today: practice a principle without mentioning it.
meditations-11.22:
Think of the country mouse and the town mouse, Marcus says, and the town mouse's fright and panic.

He's referring to Aesop's fable. The town mouse has rich food but lives in constant fear; the country mouse has simple fare and peace. Marcus, living at the center of the empire, clearly felt the point.

Today: notice one luxury that comes with anxiety attached.
meditations-11.23:
Socrates used to call the opinions of the crowd 'Lamiae', bogeymen to frighten children.

The Lamia was a monster from Greek folklore used to scare children into behaving. Socrates' joke is that public opinion works the same way: it frightens us, but it's mostly imaginary.

Today: notice one opinion you fear that's more bogeyman than real threat.
meditations-11.24:
At their public shows, Marcus says, the Spartans used to put seats in the shade for visitors, while they themselves sat anywhere.

It's a small, telling custom: hospitality to strangers, and indifference to their own comfort. It's an example of generosity and toughness together.

Today: give someone else the better seat, literally or figuratively.
meditations-11.25:
Socrates excused himself to Perdiccas, a king of Macedon, for not visiting him, Marcus says. He said he didn't want to die the worst death: receiving a favor he couldn't repay.

Socrates valued his independence too much to accept gifts that would put him in a king's debt. Being beholden can compromise you.

Today: think twice before accepting a favor that would leave you obligated in a way you'd regret.
meditations-11.26:
In the writings of one school, Marcus says (the text is uncertain, possibly the Epicureans), there was this rule: constantly keep in mind someone from the past who practiced virtue.

It's simple advice that works. Having a model in mind, a person you admire, makes it easier to act well. You can ask what they would do.

Today: pick a person you admire, and ask what they'd do in one situation you face.
meditations-11.27:
The Pythagoreans tell us, Marcus says, to look at the sky in the morning, to remember the bodies that always do the same thing in the same way, and their purity and nakedness. For there is no veil over a star.

It's a beautiful practice: start the day by looking at something steady, orderly and unhidden, and let it set the tone for your own conduct.

Today: look at the sky in the morning, and aim to be as steady and open.
meditations-11.28:
Think about Socrates, Marcus says, when he wore a skin after his wife Xanthippe had taken his cloak and gone out, and what he said to his friends who were embarrassed and drew back when they saw him dressed like that.

What Socrates said hasn't survived. But the scene shows a man unbothered by looking ridiculous, and friends more concerned about appearances than he was.

Today: let go of one worry about how you look to others.
meditations-11.29:
You can't set rules for others in writing or reading, Marcus says, before you've learned to follow rules yourself. Much more so in life.

It's a call for humility before instruction. You can't lead others to a standard you haven't met.

Today: practice one standard yourself before expecting it of anyone else.
meditations-11.30-32:
Three quotations Marcus noted down. From Euripides: 'You're a slave; free speech isn't for you.' From the Odyssey: 'And my heart laughed within,' Odysseus's silent laughter after he'd tricked the Cyclops. From Hesiod: 'And they'll curse virtue, speaking harsh words.'

Read together, they touch on freedom of speech, inner joy that doesn't need to be shown, and how good people are often abused.

The second line is the gem: a quiet inner laughter that doesn't depend on anyone noticing.

Today: let yourself enjoy one private moment of satisfaction without needing to share it.
enchiridion-47:
When you've learned to live frugally, Epictetus says, don't brag about it. If you drink only water, don't keep announcing, 'I drink water.' Remember how much more frugal and enduring the poor are than we are.

If you want to train yourself in hardship, do it for your own sake, not for show. Don't attempt dramatic feats. When you're desperately thirsty, just rinse your mouth with water and tell no one.

It's a sharp warning about virtue becoming vanity. Self-discipline loses its point the moment it becomes a performance.

Today: practice one small discipline and tell no one about it.
meditations-11.33:
Looking for a fig in winter is madness, Marcus says. So is looking for your child when that's no longer allowed.

The line comes from Epictetus. It's stark: everything has its season, including the people we love. Expecting otherwise only adds to grief. The point isn't to love less but to love knowing that nothing lasts.

Today: appreciate someone you love while they're in season.
meditations-11.34:
When you kiss your child, Epictetus said, whisper to yourself: 'Tomorrow you may die.' 'But that's an ill-omened thing to say.' 'Nothing that describes a work of nature is ill-omened,' Epictetus replied, 'or else it's ill-omened to speak of ears of grain being reaped.'

It sounds harsh, but the intent is tender. Remembering that loved ones are mortal makes the present moment more precious and the eventual loss less shattering.

Today: hug someone you love and let yourself feel how precious they are.
meditations-11.35:
The unripe grape, the ripe bunch, the raisin: all changes, Marcus says, not into nothing, but into something that doesn't yet exist.

Another line from Epictetus. Each stage of change isn't an ending but a becoming. What looks like loss is often transformation into something new.

Today: see one change in your life as becoming something, not just losing something.
meditations-11.36:
'No one can rob us of our free will.'

Another line from Epictetus, and the heart of Stoicism in nine words. Others can take your possessions, health, reputation or freedom of movement. But your choices, your judgments and your will remain yours.

Today: in one situation where you feel powerless, find the choice that's still yours.
meditations-11.37-38:
Epictetus also said, Marcus notes, that we need a method for giving our assent to impressions. Our actions should take circumstances into account, serve others, and respect each thing's real value. We should keep away from sensual desire entirely, and shouldn't feel aversion toward anything outside our control.

And the stakes? The argument, Epictetus said, isn't about some ordinary matter. It's about being sane or insane.

These are the three Stoic disciplines in brief: of judgment, of action, and of desire. Get them wrong and you're not just mistaken; you're living in a kind of madness.

Today: practice one of the three: judge carefully, act for others, or let go of a desire.
meditations-11.39:
Socrates used to say: 'What do you want, rational souls or irrational?' 'Rational.' 'Healthy or unhealthy?' 'Healthy.' 'Then why don't you seek them?' 'Because we have them.' 'Then why do you fight and quarrel?'

The dialogue has a sting in its tail. We all claim to be reasonable and sound, yet our quarrels suggest otherwise.

Today: in one disagreement, act as reasonably as you claim to be.
meditations-12.1:
Everything you hope to reach by a roundabout path, Marcus says, you can have now, if you don't deny it to yourself. That means ignoring the past, trusting the future to providence, and directing the present with reverence and justice.

Reverence, so you accept your lot, made for you as you for it. Justice, so you speak the truth freely and do what's lawful and fair. Don't let others' wickedness, opinion, talk or bodily sensations stop you.

At the end, if you honor only your mind and the divine within, and fear not death but never having begun to live by nature, you'll be worthy of the universe and no longer a stranger in your own home.

Today: stop postponing the life you want to live, and begin one part of it now.
meditations-12.2:
God sees all minds stripped of their bodily covering, Marcus says, touching only the intelligence that flowed from him into these bodies. If you train yourself to see this way, you'll free yourself of much trouble. Someone who doesn't fuss over the flesh around them won't fuss over clothes, houses, fame and other external show.

It's an invitation to see people, and yourself, as minds rather than appearances. Much anxiety about image falls away when you do.

Today: look past one person's appearance to their character.
meditations-12.3:
You're made of three things, Marcus says: a little body, a little breath, and a mind. The first two are yours to take care of; only the third is truly yours.

So separate from your mind everything others do or say, everything you've done or said, future worries, bodily sensations you didn't choose, and the swirl of outside events. Let your mind live pure and free, acting justly, accepting what happens and speaking truth. Make yourself like Empedocles' sphere, 'round and rejoicing in its rest.'

If you live only what is really your life, the present, you'll pass the rest of your days calmly, nobly, and true to the god within.

Today: set aside one worry about the past or future, and live the present.
meditations-12.4:
I've often wondered, Marcus says, how everyone loves himself more than anyone else, yet values his own opinion of himself less than other people's. If a god or a wise teacher told someone to think and plan nothing he wouldn't immediately say out loud, he couldn't bear it for a single day. That's how much more we respect what our neighbors think of us than what we think of ourselves.

It's a sharp observation about self-respect: we claim to love ourselves, but we trust others' judgment of us more than our own.

Today: let your own honest judgment of yourself count more than someone else's.
enchiridion-48:
An ordinary person, Epictetus says, expects help or harm only from outside. A philosopher expects help or harm only from himself.

The signs of someone making progress: they don't criticize, praise, blame or accuse anyone, and don't speak of themselves as being anybody or knowing anything. When blocked, they blame themselves. When praised, they quietly smile at the person praising. When criticized, they don't defend themselves.

They move carefully, like someone recovering from illness, wary of disturbing what's healing. They restrain desire, keep aversion only for what would harm their own will, act with moderation, and don't mind seeming foolish. In short, they watch themselves like an enemy lying in ambush.

Today: when praised or criticized, respond with a quiet smile rather than a reaction.
meditations-12.5:
How can it be, Marcus asks, that the gods, who arranged everything so well and kindly for us, overlooked this one thing: that very good people, closest to the divine through their lives and devotion, are completely extinguished when they die?

His answer: if it should have been otherwise, the gods would have arranged it. If it were just, it would be possible; if it were natural, nature would have done it. So if it's not so, trust that it shouldn't be. The very fact that you're arguing this with the gods presumes they're good and just, and so wouldn't neglect anything unjustly.

It's a moving passage: Marcus wrestling honestly with mortality and choosing trust.

Today: let go of one 'why' you can't answer, and trust the larger order.
meditations-12.6:
Practice even the things you despair of doing, Marcus says. The left hand is clumsy at most things for lack of practice, yet it holds the reins more firmly than the right, because it's been trained in that.

It's encouragement about skill and character alike. What seems impossible is often just unpracticed. Repetition builds capacity where there was none.

Today: practice one thing you think you're bad at.
meditations-12.7:
Think about the state, in body and soul, you should be in when death finds you, Marcus says. Think about the shortness of life, the vast gulf of time before and after, and the frailty of all matter.

It's a reflection meant to prompt readiness. If death came today, how would you want to be found? That question can reshape how you spend this day.

Today: live so that, if today were your last, you'd be content with how it found you.
meditations-12.8:
Look at the essential forms of things, Marcus says, stripped of their coverings. Look at the purposes behind actions. Consider what pain, pleasure, death and fame really are. See who is the cause of his own unease; that no one is hindered by another; that everything is opinion.

It's a compact list of Stoic exercises: see things as they are, examine motives, reassess fears and desires, and take responsibility for your own state of mind.

Today: pick one item from his list and look at it clearly.
meditations-12.9:
In applying your principles, Marcus says, be like a pancratiast, an all-in fighter, not a gladiator. A gladiator drops his sword and is killed. The other always has his hands and only needs to use them.

Principles you have to pick up and might drop are like a sword. Principles built into you are like your hands: always there, never lost.

Today: practice one principle until it feels like part of you.
meditations-12.10:
See what things really are, Marcus says, by dividing them into matter, form and purpose.

It's a short analytical tool. What is it made of? What structure or pattern makes it what it is? What is it for? Answering those three questions often deflates the hold something has on you.

Today: analyze one thing that grips you by its matter, form and purpose.
meditations-12.11:
What power a person has, Marcus says, to do nothing except what God would approve, and to accept everything God gives.

It's a statement of freedom, not constraint. You can always choose to act well, and you can always choose to accept what comes. Those two powers are enough for a good life.

Today: act well in one choice, and accept one thing gracefully.
meditations-12.12:
For what happens according to nature, Marcus says, we shouldn't blame the gods, who do nothing wrong either willingly or unwillingly, or people, who do wrong only unwillingly. So we should blame no one.

It's a radical conclusion: if no one does wrong on purpose, blame loses its point. That doesn't mean ignoring harm, but responding with correction and patience rather than accusation.

Today: go one day without blaming anyone.
meditations-12.13:
How ridiculous, Marcus says, and what a stranger to the world, is someone surprised by anything that happens in life.

Nearly everything that happens has happened before. Shock and outrage often come from forgetting that. Expecting life's ordinary troubles makes them easier to meet calmly.

Today: meet one surprise with 'of course' rather than 'how could this happen?'
enchiridion-49:
When someone shows off about understanding and explaining the books of Chrysippus, the great Stoic theorist, Epictetus says, think: if Chrysippus had written clearly, this person would have nothing to boast about.

What do I actually want? To understand nature and follow it. I look for someone to explain it. I hear Chrysippus does, so I go to him. I can't understand him, so I look for an interpreter. Nothing to be proud of so far. When I find one, what matters is putting the teaching into practice.

If I only admire the explanation, I'm a literary scholar, not a philosopher. When someone asks me to explain Chrysippus, I blush that I can't show actions that match his words.

Today: practice one idea you admire, rather than just explaining it.
meditations-12.14:
Either there is fixed necessity and unbreakable order, Marcus says, or a kindly providence that can be moved, or a chaos without purpose or guide. If there's necessity, why resist? If providence, make yourself worthy of divine help. If chaos, be glad that in such a storm you have a governing mind within you.

And if the storm carries you off, let it take the flesh, the breath and everything else. It won't carry off your mind.

It's the clearest version of his three-way argument, and it ends with something unshakeable in every case.

Today: in one chaotic moment, remember that your mind is still yours.
meditations-12.15:
Does a lamp's light shine without losing its brightness until it's put out? Marcus asks. And will the truth, justice and self-control in you go out before you do?

It's a challenge to keep your principles burning to the end. A lamp doesn't dim on its own before it's extinguished. Your character shouldn't fade before your life does.

Today: keep one principle shining even when you're tired.
meditations-12.16:
When someone seems to have done wrong, Marcus says, ask: how do I know it's wrong? And if it is, how do I know he hasn't already condemned himself, which is like tearing his own face?

Wanting a bad person not to do wrong is like wanting a fig tree not to have juice, babies not to cry, or horses not to neigh. What else would someone of that character do? If you're irritated, work on curing that person's disposition.

It's a call to replace irritation with understanding and, where possible, help.

Today: when you see someone do wrong, consider that they may already regret it.
meditations-12.17:
'If it isn't right, don't do it. If it isn't true, don't say it.' The passage breaks off after this in the original.

Two rules that cover a great deal of life. They don't require complex reasoning, just honesty about whether something is right and whether something is true.

Today: apply both rules to everything you do and say.
meditations-12.18:
Always look at what's producing an impression in you, Marcus says, and break it down into its form, its matter, its purpose, and the time within which it must end.

It's an analytical habit for staying calm. When something stirs you up, dissecting it into parts, and remembering it has a limited lifespan, reduces its power.

Today: dissect one strong impression into its parts.
meditations-12.19:
Realize at last, Marcus says, that you have something in you better and more divine than the things that stir your emotions and jerk you around like a puppet. What's in my mind right now: fear, suspicion, desire, something like that?

It's a call to self-awareness. Stopping to name what's driving you is the first step to taking back control.

Today: stop three times and name what emotion is pulling your strings.
meditations-12.20:
First, do nothing thoughtlessly or without purpose, Marcus says. Second, let your actions aim at nothing but the common good.

Two rules: act deliberately, and act for others. Between them they cover most of what Marcus asks of himself in the whole book.

Today: before each significant action, ask what it's for and who it helps.
meditations-12.21:
Before long you'll be nobody and nowhere, Marcus says, and neither will anything you see now, or anyone now alive. Everything is made to change, turn and perish, so that other things can follow in succession.

It's not meant to depress but to clarify. Change and ending make room for new life. You're part of a continuous succession, not its center.

Today: see your life as one link in a long chain, and make it a good one.
meditations-12.22:
Remember that everything is opinion, Marcus says, and opinion is in your power. Remove your opinion whenever you choose, and like a sailor who has rounded the headland, you'll find calm, everything still, and a bay without waves.

It's one of the book's most beautiful images. The storm is often in your judgment; change the judgment and you're in calm water.

Today: when you feel tossed about, change one judgment and see if the water calms.
enchiridion-50:
Whatever principles you've adopted, Epictetus says, keep them like laws you'd be wrong to break, and ignore what people say about you.

How long will you put off demanding the best of yourself? You've learned the principles. What teacher are you waiting for? You're not a child. If you keep procrastinating, setting one date after another to start, you'll make no progress and live and die ordinary.

Right now, consider yourself worthy of living as a grown adult making progress. When pain or pleasure, glory or disgrace confronts you, remember: the contest is now, the Olympics have begun, and you can't postpone them. One defeat can lose your progress, or one effort can save it.

That's how Socrates became who he was. You're not Socrates yet, but you can live as someone trying to become him.

Today: stop waiting, and start the change you've been putting off.
meditations-12.23:
Any activity that stops at its proper time suffers no harm by stopping, Marcus says, and neither does the person who did it. So life, the whole series of our acts, suffers no harm by ending at its proper time, and the person isn't wronged.

Nature sets the time, sometimes through old age, always through the universal order, whose constant change keeps the whole world young and complete. What serves the whole is always good and timely.

So death is no evil. It isn't shameful, since it's beyond our will and doesn't harm the common good. It's even good, because it's timely and fits the whole.

Today: let one thing end at its proper time without resisting.
meditations-12.24:
Keep three principles ready, Marcus says. First, act only thoughtfully and justly; as for what comes from outside, it comes from chance or providence, and you shouldn't blame chance or accuse providence.

Second, think of what every being is from seed to receiving a soul, and from that to giving it back: what it's made of and what it dissolves into.

Third, imagine being lifted above the earth and seeing human affairs in all their variety, along with all the beings in the air and sky. However often you rose, you'd see the same: sameness of form and shortness of life. Is that something to be proud of?

Today: practice the view from above on one thing you're proud or anxious about.
meditations-12.25:
'Throw away your opinion, and you are saved. Who stops you throwing it away?'

It's Marcus at his most concise. The judgments that torment us are ours to discard. The question at the end is a challenge: nothing outside you is forcing you to keep them.

Today: throw away one opinion that's troubling you.
meditations-12.26:
When you're troubled, Marcus says, you've forgotten something. That everything happens by nature. That another's wrong is nothing to you. That everything that happens always has and always will, everywhere. How close the kinship is between each person and all humanity, a kinship not of blood but of mind.

You've forgotten that each person's mind is a god, flowing from the divine. That nothing is truly yours; your child, your body and your soul came from God. That everything is opinion. And that each person lives only in the present, and loses only that.

It's a list of remedies you can run through when upset.

Today: when troubled, ask which of these you've forgotten.
meditations-12.27:
Keep remembering people who complained bitterly about things, Marcus says, or were famous for fortune, disaster, feuds or anything else. Where are they now? Smoke, ash and a story, or not even that.

Think of how Fabius Catullinus lived in the country, Lucius Lupus in his gardens, Stertinius at Baiae, the emperor Tiberius on Capri, and Velius Rufus. Think of all eager pursuits mixed with pride, and how worthless everything is that people strain after.

It's more philosophical to be just, self-controlled and reverent, simply. Because pride that's proud of having no pride is the most unbearable of all.

Today: do one good thing simply, without even being proud of your humility.
meditations-12.28:
To those who ask, 'Where have you seen the gods, or how do you know they exist, that you worship them?' Marcus answers: first, they can be seen even with the eyes, meaning the heavens; second, I haven't seen my own soul either, yet I honor it. So with the gods: from what I constantly experience of their power, I know they exist, and I revere them.

It's an honest, modest answer. He doesn't claim proof, only that what he experiences is enough to warrant reverence, just as he trusts his own mind without seeing it.

Today: notice one thing you trust without seeing it directly.
meditations-12.29:
The security of life, Marcus says, is this: examine everything thoroughly, what it is, its matter and its form; do justice with your whole soul and speak the truth. What remains but to enjoy life by joining one good act to the next, leaving no gap between them?

It's a joyful conclusion: life's real pleasure isn't in rest or reward, but in a continuous chain of good actions.

Today: link one good action to the next, without a gap.
meditations-12.30:
There's one light of the sun, Marcus says, though walls and mountains break it up. One substance, though spread across countless bodies. One soul, though divided among countless natures. One intelligent soul, though it seems divided.

The other parts, air and matter, have no feeling or fellowship, yet the intelligent principle holds them together too. But mind has a special pull toward its own kind, joins with it, and the feeling of fellowship is never cut off.

It's a vision of human connection as part of the structure of reality. We seem separate, but we share one light.

Today: treat someone you disagree with as sharing the same light as you.
meditations-12.31:
What do you want? Marcus asks. To keep existing? To feel, move, grow, then stop growing, speak and think? Which of these seems worth longing for? If it's easy to value them lightly, turn to what's left: following reason and God. But it's inconsistent with honoring reason and God to be troubled that death will take the rest away.

It's a clarifying question. If the things death takes aren't what you value most, then death takes nothing that matters most.

Today: ask what you'd most hate to lose, and whether death could really take it.
meditations-12.32:
How tiny a share of boundless time is given to each person, Marcus says, soon swallowed by eternity. How small a share of all substance, of the universal soul, and on what a little clod of the earth you creep!

Thinking about this, consider nothing great except acting as your nature leads and enduring what common nature brings.

It's near the end of the book, and he returns to his oldest theme: perspective. Against the scale of things, only acting well and enduring well are great.

Today: measure one worry against the size of the universe, then act well anyway.
enchiridion-51:
The first and most necessary part of philosophy, Epictetus says, is applying principles, like 'don't lie'. The second is proving them: why not lie? The third is checking the proofs: what makes a proof valid? The third serves the second, and the second the first. But we do the opposite: we spend all our time on the third, neglect the first, and lie while explaining why lying is wrong.

He ends with lines to keep at hand. From Cleanthes: 'Lead me, Zeus, and you, Destiny, wherever you've assigned me; I'll follow gladly, and if I refuse, I'll follow anyway.' From Euripides: whoever yields well to fate is wise. And from Plato's Socrates: 'If it pleases the gods, so be it,' and 'Anytus and Meletus can kill me, but they cannot harm me.'

Today: put one principle into practice instead of debating it.
meditations-12.33:
How does the ruling faculty use itself? Marcus asks. That's everything. All the rest, whether in your power or not, is lifeless ashes and smoke.

Near the end of the book, he narrows his focus to a single point: how you use your own mind. Everything else is secondary.

Today: pay attention to how you're using your mind, more than to what's happening around you.
meditations-12.34:
This thought helps most to make us look down on death, Marcus says: even people who think pleasure is good and pain is evil have still faced death with contempt.

He means the Epicureans, who prized pleasure yet didn't fear death. If even those who value pleasure most can meet death calmly, surely a Stoic can.

Today: think of someone who faced a hard end bravely, and let it steady you.
meditations-12.35:
For someone to whom only what comes in its proper season is good, Marcus says, to whom it doesn't matter whether they've done more or fewer right acts, and who doesn't care whether they get to contemplate the world for longer or shorter, death isn't terrible.

It's a portrait of someone free from counting: not tallying good deeds, not measuring life's length. Such a person lives fully in the present and has nothing to fear from the end.

Today: stop counting one thing you measure your life by, and just live it well.
meditations-12.36:
The last passage of the Meditations. You've been a citizen of this great city, the world, Marcus says. What difference does it make whether for five years or three? What's lawful is fair to everyone. Where's the hardship if you're sent away not by a tyrant or an unjust judge, but by nature, who brought you in? It's like a magistrate dismissing an actor he hired.

'But I've only played three of the five acts.' True, but in life three acts can be the whole play. The one who composed it, and now dissolves it, decides when it's complete, and you're the cause of neither.

'So go in peace, for the one who releases you is at peace too.' It's a calm, generous ending: no protest, just gratitude.

Today: treat today as a complete act, whatever comes next.
